⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
  • Industry observers note that whisk 1 tsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Industry observers note that whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

It has been revealed that turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

In a recent development, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

It has been revealed that place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

In a recent development, unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#146301. The 20 Most Iconic Colognes of All Time, According to GQ in 2026

The 20 Most Iconic Colognes of All Time, According to GQ in 2026

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece.
  • All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years.
  • Our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece. Well, as a longtime fragrance editor, I get a similar feeling when I smell Guerlain’s iconic Vétiver scent (or, more recently, Penhaligon’s Halfeti). These fragrances smelled exceptional when they debuted, still do today, probably still will a hundred years from now. And while fragrance, like any art form, has its trends, the truly great scents (and songs) have a way of deflecting them and singing on.

All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years. To do so, I dug through the history of men’s fragrance to put together a list of some of the most iconic colognes of all time. Scents that defined an era, changed the course of perfumery, or smelled so good that folks never stopped wearing them.

Our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time. You might love some more than others, but all have earned their place in the fragrance pantheon. Here are 20 of the most popular, influential, and enduring colognes ever made, and exactly why they’ve lasted.

According to recent reports, is there a more classic cologne than Acqua di Parma’s Colonia? Launched in 1916, this timeless citrus is the original Italian splash, and it would be criminal not to include it on a list of this caliber. That crisp, bright citrus opening is unmistakable, but there’s so much more going on beneath the surface as it dries down, with the supporting notes weaving in and out without ever stealing the show. Herbaceous hints of lavender and rosemary add herbal hues, while earthy vetiver and patchouli mingle with the smooth warmth of sandalwood as it settles on the skin. This is one of the great daily drivers, if not the very archetype of what an everyday cologne could or should be. It’s a 10/10 blend of citrus, aromatics, and woods, and more than a century on, still smells as sophisticated as ever.

In a recent development, I’ve written about Guerlain Vétiver so many times, you’d think I’d have run out of ways to sing its praises. But I could go forever. Few fragrances have done more to establish vetiver as a leading note, and since its 1959 debut, this masterpiece has remained every bit as relevant and wearable. It beautifully captures vetiver’s fresher, greener side, rather than leaning into its smoky, earthy character. There’s a crispness, with bright citrus, a touch of spice, and grassy vetiver balanced by subtle tobacco and woods, like the first cool, earthy dew on a spring morning. Elegant and confident, it oozes the kind of sophistication I imagine old-school Hollywood leading men appreciating, yet it wears just as well today, whether you're suited up or simply going about your day.

Ask me to name the most influential luxury fragrance of the 21st century, and there’s a good chance I’d say Aventus (notice, I mentioned “luxury”). I’ve seen firsthand just how many guys made their first foray into high-end fragrance with this icon, and while I now often gravitate toward some of the deeper cuts in Creed’s storied catalog, every time I wear Aventus, the compliments roll in. Since its 2010 debut, it has inspired countless imitators and the inevitable fragrance fatigue that comes with being a phenomenon, yet I don’t think it’s lost an ounce of its appeal. To me, it's the ultimate wedding fragrance, a perfect blend of bright citrus and pineapple, aromatic freshness, and rich, smoky woods that’s refined without being fussy. The defining fragrance of the 2010s? I’d make that argument any day. Aventus will always have a place on my shelf.

It has been revealed that no. 89 is one of the great British gentlemen’s fragrances, and few colognes capture Bond-like elegance quite like it. And it tracks: Introduced in 1951, No. 89 counted James Bond creator Ian Fleming among its famous admirers, while Cary Grant and Sir Alec Guinness were reportedly devotees as well. The scent itself is traditional in the best way, a classically composed fougère with crisp, almost barbershop-like citrus and lavender freshness, subtle florals, warming spice, and a smooth, woody base of vetiver and oakmoss. Aromatic, gently spicy, and impeccably polished, it’s the olfactory equivalent of a beautifully tailored Savile Row suit. More than seven decades on, No. 89 is proof that class and character never go out of style.

According to recent reports, back in the ’90s, CK One was everywhere. From Wall Street execs to flannel-wearing creatives; its intoxicating freshness just captured the zeitgeist. It was also one of the first mainstream fragrances marketed as unisex. (Almost an afterthought for fragrance fans today, it was a fairly novel concept then.) And while countless fragrances have followed in its footsteps, this citrusy, green, woodsy, lightly sweet profile still more than holds up. A surprising amount is going on here, too: a bright medley of citrus and tropical fruits, a floral heart with hints of spice, and a clean, musky base of cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s an icon that helped define a generation, and it works just as well day or night, on pretty much anyone. And perhaps most impressively, after all these years, CK One still smells unmistakably like CK One.

According to recent reports, much like his clothing, Ralph Lauren’s original Polo fragrance has left an indelible mark on American style. Debuted in 1978, the unmistakable green-bottled cologne helped define what a classic masculine fragrance could smell like: sophisticated, confident, and unapologetically aromatic. And while nearly five decades have passed, there’s still nothing quite like it. That signature pine-heavy character is front and center, surrounded by a rich blend of herb and spices with bergamot adding brightness and leather lending rugged, earthy depth. It’s bold, woody, green, and distinctly old-school, but that’s precisely its charm. It’s undergone reformulations over the years, and its assertive character won’t appeal to everyone, but there’s no denying its place in the fragrance hall of fame. Some colognes come and go, but Polo isn’t going anywhere.

It has been revealed that when I spotted that frosted bottle in my dad’s medicine cabinet and wore it for the first time, I had no idea that this scent would spark a lifelong fragrance obsession. Armani’s 1996 icon, Acqua di Giò, has been worn by millions, referenced endlessly, and spawned countless flankers, but the original remains one of those rare mass-appeal designer colognes that have stood the test of time. Why? Because it’s just so wearable. Long before the niche fragrance boom, when designer colognes dominated department store counters, Acqua di Giò caught on like wildfire, appealing to just about every kind of guy, whether for the office or date night. At its core is a beautifully nuanced blend of citrus, fresh marine accords, and soft florals, grounded by a musky amber base. On skin, it’s breezy, clean, and subtly woody, with an oceanic quality. If you’ve never rocked it or haven’t reached for it in years, do yourself a favor and revisit this classic.

According to recent reports, imitation is the highest form of flattery, and so many colognes still try to smell like Cool Water. Introduced in 1988, it became a full-blown phenomenon in the ’90s, and for a generation of guys, it was practically a rite of passage. Along with CK One, it was non-negotiable during my formative years, and even then, before I’d developed my own distinct taste, I knew I didn’t want to smell like everyone else. But there was something about this intoxicating green aquatic I just couldn’t resist. Its blend of lavender, mint, rosemary, and neroli nodded to classic gentleman’s fougères, but Cool Water took that aromatic DNA somewhere fresh—a singular scent that’s herbal and richly marine, softened by a woody, musky warmth. While it might smell dated to some, there’s no denying its place among the most iconic fragrances of all time, and I’d argue it still smells amazing on the right dude, especially on a spring or summer day.

Terre d’Hermès is (probably) my favorite designer fragrance of all time. When Jean-Claude Ellena created it back in 2006, he delivered something entirely different from the crowd-pleasing designer colognes of the day. There’s an earthiness to it that I find irresistible, a marriage of citrus, dry woods, spice, and that unmistakable flinty, mineral character that gives it so much personality. It’s sophisticated without being stuffy, with a gorgeous, almost boozy warmth that makes it feel sultry and downright sexy. I particularly love wearing it in colder weather, when those warm, woody facets really come alive, but I can reach for it almost anytime. Plenty of designer colognes are simply pleasant, but Terre d’Hermès is distinctive and endlessly wearable.

Industry observers note that few colognes in modern history have generated as much conversation, inspired as many memes, or become quite as zeitgeist-y as Dior Sauvage. Love it or roll your eyes at its popularity, its influence on modern men’s perfumery is undeniable. Since its debut in 2015, Sauvage has become one of the world’s bestselling fragrances, at times even claiming the number-one spot. And it’s easy to see why. That unmistakable blend of citrus, spice, and all things ambery nice is crisp and fresh, with a warm, woody drydown that’s oh so smooth. It’s a crowd-pleaser in the truest sense, versatile enough to wear just about anywhere, though I think it really shines after dark. Sauvage has since spawned an entire family of flankers, but the original EDT started it all.

You've smelled Bleu de Chanel on plenty of guys. A beautifully composed citrus-spice-wood classic, it works just as well with a navy suit as it does with a white tee and jeans. Note: When Chanel's legendary perfumer Jacques Polge introduced it in 2010, he didn't just create another handsome, crowd-pleasing cologne; he helped define the modern blue fragrance, a fresh, clean, citrusy, and woody genre that's become a mainstay. Sixteen years on, the original remains one of the most approachable and endlessly versatile colognes ever. Its bright citrus opening gives way to an aromatic blend of cool mint, warming spices, and subtle florals, all grounded by a rich, woody base with touches of earthy vetiver, patchouli, and resinous warmth. There really is only one Bleu.

Industry observers note that this was a tough call. Ask any scent head about Tom Ford's fragrances, and they’ll surely bring up Neroli Portofino and Tobacco Vanille, both arguably just as iconic (and good) as this one. But if you polled fans on the most influential Tom Ford fragrances, I think Oud Wood would edge out the competition. Launched in 2007, it helped introduce Oud to a broader Western audience, making the traditionally intense ingredient feel approachable. It’s elegant and beautifully blended, with a smoky, almost creamy heart of oud, sandalwood, and rosewood, accented by subtle spice and the warmth of vanilla and amber. It’s heady yet easy to wear, with an addictive richness that never wears thin.

Sources indicate that I’ve worn pretty much every Le Labo under the sun, and while my personal favorites lean toward the eucalyptus and vetiver side of the house, there’s simply no telling the story of modern perfumery without Santal 33. Love it or find it utterly overplayed, you’ve smelled it. Since its 2011 debut, it’s wafted through elevators, the backseats of cabs, countless weddings and date nights, and just about everywhere in between. More importantly, it helped bring sandalwood into the mainstream, and became a reference point for an entire genre of warm, woody fragrances. But before everyone started rocking it, Santal 33 was, and still is, a brilliant composition: creamy sandalwood, dry cedar, cardamom spice, and leathery warmth. It’s a niche legend that has suffered from its own success, yes, but give it another ten years, and don’t be surprised if the very fragrance many got tired of smelling becomes cool all over again.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re remotely a scent head, chances are you dig at least one, if not several, of Parfums de Marly’s fragrances (my personal favorite is the oud-praline magic that is Haltane). But if I had to sum up the house in one word, it would be regal. It does refined, layered elegance exceptionally well, and while some folks might champion Althaïr or Castley, to my nose, the fougère-forward Layton best epitomizes the house. Launched in 2016, it’s one of the finest fougères I’ve ever smelled, rich yet airy, with classic lavender reimagined alongside crisp apple, bright citrus, cardamom, woods, and a healthy dose of vanilla. It’s practically the template for what a modern fougère aspires to be, and its enduring popularity suggests plenty of fragrance fans would agree. It doesn’t hurt that the matte blue bottle with its signature silver dome is so flauntworthy.

In a recent development, few fragrances in recent times have had the same cultural impact as Baccarat Rouge 540, becoming a signature scent for everyone from socialites to fragrance obsessives. Yes, it's polarizing, and some might argue its ubiquity has stripped it of some of its magic. But it's become a modern classic for a reason, starting with the masterful nose behind it: Francis Kurkdjian, founder of his namesake maison. Launched in 2015, it's a luminous floral amber, with saffron lending spice, jasmine bringing a soft warmth, and a generous dose of amberwood creating that glowing aura. Sultry, heady, and diffusive, it's a straight-up unisex phenomenon that smells a little different on everyone who wears it, yet still announces itself before you even enter a room. Whether you're a devotee or a detractor, there's no denying it's left its mark.

It has been revealed that it came down to Bal d’Afrique and Gypsy Water, though plenty of Byredo fragrances could have earned a spot here. But I’m the editor, and I’m going with my all-time favorite from one of the houses that helped bring niche perfumery into the mainstream. Rolled out in 2008, Gypsy Water was one of the first niche fragrances I ever fell for, and it holds such a special place in my heart that I still wear it regularly. There’s something almost holy about its airy blend of incense, soft woods, bright lemon, and a whisper of vanilla and amber, all coming together with that subtle yet magnetic, almost skin-scent quality Byredo does so well. Artsy, chic, and easy to love, this woody aromatic never tries too hard to make an impression yet often leaves a lasting one.

Since its 2015 debut, Xerjoff’s Naxos has achieved near-mythic status, winning over everyone from fragrance-obsessed TikTokers to yacht-owning gentlemen with decidedly expensive taste. And I get it. This is an almost impossibly well-blended composition that somehow manages to be both decadent and incredibly wearable, making it a great place to start if you’re looking to venture into niche perfumery. On paper, the combination of tobacco, aromatic lavender, fruity freshness, and a prominent honey accord sounds like it shouldn’t quite work, but man, does it ever. That rich sweetness is a defining feature, especially in the opening, before the herbal, earthy tones and a hefty dose of vanilla come together in a downright sumptuous yet crisp way. The hype may have quieted down since its social media heyday, but Naxos deserves its flowers as a modern niche standout.

According to recent reports, halfeti has become a signature of mine, though I’m admittedly a little late to the game, having received my first bottle as a birthday gift last year, well after it had achieved iconic status in scent circles. But better late than never, especially when a fragrance is this good. Named after a Turkish town known for its roses, it leans into a rich, heady floral style, layered with citrus, herbs, and spice. Bergamot and grapefruit lift the opening before saffron and cardamom give way to a deep base of leather, oud, cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s a lot, but it all hangs together gorgeously, creating a woody, spicy, aromatic scent that’s elegant and sexy, perfect for special occasions or date nights. But I’d happily wear it just about anywhere, including when I’m not going anywhere at all.

Recent findings suggest that musc Ravageur embodies the risk-taking spirit of niche perfumery. Rolled out in 2000, it helped redefine what a modern musk fragrance could be at a time when fresh, clean fragrances dominated the men’s market. More than a quarter century later, it remains a cult favorite, thanks in no small part to its warm, almost funky (in a good way) richness. It opens with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and rose, all resting on a base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. A benchmark for animalic musks, it’s an alluring, sultry, and unapologetically sensual aroma, equally suited to being a signature scent or an olfactory companion for wherever the evening leads.

According to recent reports, amouage has dropped so many olfactory bangers over the years that choosing just one for this list wasn't easy. The Omani house has built its reputation on rich, complex compositions that keep you coming back to sniff your pulse points, and while I could make a case for several of its fragrances, Reflection Man feels quintessentially Amouage. Debuted in 2007, it’s become a luxury niche benchmark, proving that a floral-forward fragrance can be every bit as rich and sophisticated as its woody or spicy counterparts. It opens with an herbaceous blend of rosemary, berries, and orange before orris, jasmine, and ylang-ylang bring a lush, earthy depth, all grounded by a smooth base of vetiver, patchouli, and sandalwood. The result is a layered floral-woody scent that’s distinctive without being difficult to wear, and versatile enough for everything from a boardroom to a black-tie gala. Pricey, yes, but worth every spritz.

Blade Runner 2099 Ends on a Touching Note About Empathy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that blade Runner 2099 might not be getting a second season, but the show’s final episode provided a tidy ending for everyone involved.
  • Recent findings suggest that the journey isn’t without its twists and turns: One person who is the key to obtaining Tyrell’s memory winds up dead, and Olwen’s future hangs in the balance as she gets closer to the end of her lifespan.
  • Here’s what happened in the season finale of Blade Runner 2099.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that blade Runner 2099 might not be getting a second season, but the show’s final episode provided a tidy ending for everyone involved. The final episode sees the show’s main characters, Cora and Olwen (played by Hunter Schafer and Michelle Yeoh, respectively) reaching the Tyrell Launch Complex on a quest to find out where Tyrell’s memory is located.

Recent findings suggest that the journey isn’t without its twists and turns: One person who is the key to obtaining Tyrell’s memory winds up dead, and Olwen’s future hangs in the balance as she gets closer to the end of her lifespan. Cora’s life as a Replicant also has a few complications of its own, too.

Here’s what happened in the season finale of Blade Runner 2099.

Olwen and Cora spend a large portion of the final episode searching for Tyrell’s memory at the Tyrell Launch Complex, which belongs to replicant creator Eldon Tyrell and serves as documentation about Nexus-1 replicants Julius and Helena.

Recent findings suggest that inside the complex, Olwen and Cora split up. Olwen finds Clotilde and they talk about how Julius killed her. When Clotilde suffers a fall, Olwen doesn’t allow her to die again; in exchange for saving her, Clotilde shares where Julius is within the complex.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Julius discovers Cora’s whereabouts in the complex. Shortly after, Julius and Cora fight, and he inflicts a serious stab wound on her. He also destroys Tyrell’s memory and insists that he’s the only one who can extend Olwen’s life, but Olwen finds the pair, jumps in, and kills Julius with a gunshot.

In a recent development, olwen spends the majority of the series aware that she’s at the end of her lifespan. As a Replicant, she was given a fixed limit to how long she can live and has accepted her fate—but she’s offered a second chance at life by the end of the series.

After saving Clotilde, she later reveals that she saw Tyrell’s memory before he died and knows how to re-create Olwen as a Nexus-1. Clotilde re-creates Olwen in exchange for Olwen having saved Clotilde’s life. By the end of the episode, Olwen emerges from a birthing bag, and she later leaves Earth on a spaceship.

Recent findings suggest that the series ends with Cora and Greta understanding each other. Cora, a human posing as a Replicant, heads back to LAPD and is given a Replicant test by Greta to confirm her identity, but this time, Cora turns the questions on Greta and asks about her life.

The pair talks about Greta’s doll, leading Cora to come to the realization that the girl is still capable of understanding what it means to love and be loved. Cora becomes emotional at the realization, leading Greta to comment that Cora has high levels of empathy. This means Cora technically fails the Replicant test, but Greta allows her to continue hiding her identity and her work as a Replicant.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

Recent findings suggest that the long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? Because the game was so highly anticipated that food delivery apps saw noticeable spikes in demand as players stayed home, many skipping work to play the game for hours at a time without breaks for cooking. A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.).

This is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

In other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a upcoming study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

At Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”.

In a recent development, the gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the tech giant imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

In a recent development, origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its major flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

It has been revealed that semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a upcoming study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, intends to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

According to recent reports, when I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll rapidly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

Recent findings suggest that as a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

At Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Industry observers note that preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Industry observers note that arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

When the Polish jewelry designer Natalia Kopiszka was planning her August 2026 wedding to actor Aleksander “Olek” Kaleta, she found herself at a bridal fashion crossroads, stuck between two stylistic pillars of her own brand: vintage and modern.

It has been revealed that first, the Warsaw-based designer of Kopi traveled to Paris to shop for a vintage wedding dress, but returned home empty-handed. “I didn’t find anything that I liked, so I thought: I will design my own wedding dress,” Natalia states.

For the body of her ceremony dress, she ordered fabric—silk taffeta—from Etsy. “I was on a mission to find the absolute dream silk fabric,” she indicates. “I started by checking out local fabric shops and silk wholesalers, but I just couldn't find the right silk taffeta with that delicate, subtle sheen anywhere.” She searched online and stumbled upon a listing from a Upcoming York-based seller, which she ordered on the spot. Luckily, “it turned out to be even more breathtaking in person than in the photos,” she says.

According to recent reports, then, on a weekend trip to Amsterdam with a friend, she wandered into a vintage store where she found antique lace, which she used for the bodice detailing. “The lace is truly unique because it dates back to the early 20th century, and I only had a tiny piece of it—which happened to be just enough to trim the bodice,” Natalia says. “It was such a special way to check off the ‘something old’ tradition.” She sketched the dress, then shared her designs with a dressmaker who sewed it, making her vintage-modern dream a reality.

Industry observers note that natalia and Olek first met in February 2021 at a house party in Warsaw. “For me, it was love at first sight,” Natalia recalls. “A friend of mine who lived in the apartment below me threw a get-together, and her roommate happened to be friends with Olek. As soon as he walked in, we instantly locked eyes. I’m pretty sure he was the one who came over and started the conversation first,” she adds. “It also turned out that Olek lived directly across the street from my apartment, so we used to wave at each other from our windows. Ever since that night, we started seeing each other almost every single day.”.

After a year, they moved in together in Warsaw. In 2024, Olek proposed to Natalia during a trip to Italy, in the coastal town of Polignano a Mare. “It was a warm, romantic evening with a huge moon, and surprisingly, I didn't see it coming at all,” Natalia says. “It turned out to be such a sweet, funny moment because neither of us could stop laughing.”.

On August 8, 2026, the couple held their wedding at Pałac Pstrokonie, a historic 19th-century palace in a small village outside of Warsaw. They worked with the wedding planner Kasia Fastyn, who brought Natalia’s vision—a romantic, whimsical wonderland of sorts—to life, pairing them with the event studio MyBigDay, who designed the florals and draped their dancing tent in pink fabric.

Sources indicate that as a jewelry and accessories designer, Natalia zeroed in on all the details of her wedding looks from the beginning. She knew she didn’t want a traditional floral bouquet, for example, so she opted for a small silk bag in the shape of a bouquet from the Latest York-based designer Camille Albertine, after finding her work on Instagram. Albertine custom-made Natalia’s bouquet purse in the same fabric as her dress. “Everyone was so surprised that I didn’t have a typical bouquet,” Natalia says. “It’s versatile enough that I can wear it with everyday outfits. It’s going to stay with me for a long time, and I’ll even be able to pass it down through generations.”.

According to recent reports, for her reception look, the bride changed into a dress by the Polish designer Magda Butrym, pairing it with an unexpected accessory: a crochet veil cap that her sister made. “It was a really simple dress, also silk, but I put something really crazy on my head,” Natalia states.

Natalia incorporated her own jewelry into the crochet cap-like veil, which was bedazzled with charms and pendants. “They are specially made charms with little lobster clasps so you can clip them onto the crochet work however you like. They’re gold-plated and feature Swarovski crystals,” Natalia notes. (Charms are a signature of Natalia’s brand, she explains, so it was only fitting to work them into her bridal looks.) Her love of historical pieces, particularly from the Victorian era, inspired the final design, which included blue stones for her “something blue.” A look inspired by it is now for sale as part of Kopi’s “I Do” bridal line.

According to recent reports, the bride also made Olek a pocket square with the same vintage lace as her dress, so they were matching (and so he had “something old” as well). They completed their looks with wedding bands that Natalia designed. “Mine has a retro feel, crafted in gold and set with 12 small diamonds,” she states of the rings. “Olek went for a classic look—a simple, wide gold band with my nickname engraved on the inside.” Reflecting on the wedding months later, Natalia says: “Everything was perfect.”.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Sources indicate that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Sources indicate that whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

In a recent development, transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Recent findings suggest that drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Sources indicate that do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

Yelp searches for “bakeries near me” are up 561% from last year, while searches for a “sweet treat” are up 303%. Treat yo’ self culture is officially here.

Bakery tourism is on the rise, and honestly, I'm not surprised. I, myself, am prone to walking unfamiliar city streets just to get my hands on the town's most beloved pastry. And people are getting pretty specific about what they want. Searches for cardamom buns are up 24%, kouign-amann 67%, and salt bread a whopping 616%.

Bakeries are also the most-saved type of specialty food shop on Yelp’s My Lists feature. Even New York City's Radio Bakery, which you’ll find below, saw searches increase by 176%. It seems we’re all doing some serious research before our next pastry run.

Industry observers note that so which hot spots should you add to your must-visit list? I asked Yelp to do a deep dive into the most-saved bakeries across America to see which ones people are bookmarking. Here's what came out on top.

Sources indicate that this famed Taiwanese bakery opened its first U.S. outpost earlier this year in Pasadena, California, and has already gone viral for its unique cream cheese-filled bagels and flaky pastries.

In a recent development, what started out as a pandemic-era creation has now morphed into a line-worthy brick-and-mortar. Bad Butter regularly draws block-long lines, with its breads, croissants, and pastries often selling out.

In Santa Ana, California, 61hundred Bread is known for its signature heirloom blue-corn masa sourdough bread, along with Filipino baked goods like pandesal and ube-filled cruffins.

It has been revealed that at this New York City French bakery, the jambon-beurre sandwich is the star item. Fresh baguettes and flaky croissants are also among the other reasons locals and tourists flock to the shop.

Located at the Halepuna Waikiki hotel in Honolulu, Hawaii, Halekulani Bakery is known for its signature coconut cake and assortment of pastries.

Located in Los Angeles, California, Out Of Ordi specializes in Korean-style salt bread.

New York City’s Sunday Morning frequently sells out of its viral cinnamon rolls.

San Diego’s Relic Bakery & Kitchen offers a mix of sweet and savory baked goods, from pies and croissants to breads and danishes.

In Upcoming York City, you’ll find Justin’s Salt Bread, voted the city’s best new bakery of the year and known for—you guessed it—its salt bread.

San Francisco’s Butter & Crumble is known for its crumble cakes and laminated pastries, with offerings that rotate seasonally.

Another Honolulu bakery makes the list, although this one comes with a twist. Part bakery, part butcher shop, The Local General Store sells everything from quiche and danishes to sausage and ham.

It looks like my travel schedule just got a little busier (and tastier).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting.
  • One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

Industry observers note that the other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

Yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

According to recent reports, this is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

This recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

Butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

Industry News: Why Is Fashion So Obsessed With Distressing?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in 2026, the runways are ripe with notes of distressing and deconstruction.
  • With 2008 fashion on the rise, too, maybe we’re closer than we ever thought to going back to ripped jeans.
  • Sources indicate that but why is fashion obsessed with looking worn out right now?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in 2026, the runways are ripe with notes of distressing and deconstruction. For fall/winter 2026, Prada sent crystal-covered embellished heels down the runway with perfectly pointed toes that looked as if they had just accidentally graced a puddle of distinctly dirty Fresh York City rainwater. The same is true for the label’s menswear collections: deliberate stains, frayed fabrics, and wrinkles were intentional and core to the aesthetic. At Miu Miu and Coach, leathers were aged. And for spring/summer 2027, Louis Vuitton, Gucci, Valentino, Diesel, and JW Anderson showcased elements of worn-in style, with damaged, repaired, dirty, and distressed looks dominating. After seasons of quiet luxury defined by minimal, poised, and perfected aesthetics, something about fashion’s new love affair with mess feels refreshing.

With 2008 fashion on the rise, too, maybe we’re closer than we ever thought to going back to ripped jeans. Ann Demeulemeester, Balenciaga, and Diesel seem to think so, as all of these labels put frayed jeans on the runway for the spring/summer 2027 season. Ann Demeulemeester creative director Stefano Gallici brainstormed his new collection on a journey through the Californian desert, and in the show notes mentioned intentional wear, via “Ceremony tailoring worn to death, or to eternity.”.

Sources indicate that but why is fashion obsessed with looking worn out right now? Valerie Steele, director and chief curator of The Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology, thinks there’s never been a better time for it. “There is kind of a crisis in fashion right now,” she tells ELLE. “Fashion has started to seem really out of touch with real life and real people.” One example: luxury fashion’s pricing is so high right now that some brands, like Gucci, have revealed that they’ll be reducing prices by as much as 30 percent. Also: “There is kind of more of an interest in what ‘real people’ wear. You know, what does it mean to be authentic? I mean, in many ways, I would say that authenticity is a chimera. You know, it’s a mythical beast that doesn’t really exist in a totally commodified, late capitalist world,” indicates Steele.

Sources indicate that steele notes the damaged jeans of the Y2K era, ’90s grunge moments, and earlier punk movements as similar examples. Deliberate distressing has also been famously done and documented by some of the greats, like Vivienne Westwood, Rei Kawakubo, and even Alber Elbaz, also coinciding with unique moments in time when economics and politics made it all the more interesting and, in some cases, ironic. “Fashion is supposed to be new and transgressive,” says Steele. “So, if scuffing your shoes is gonna make them more fashionable, then you go for it, right?”.

Intentionally distressed, messy fashion has been around for hundreds of years, however. “We also saw it actually with some male dandies in the second half of the 19th century,” notes Steele. “You also had some of that sensibility in New England in the late 19th century when wealthy people in Boston would go to Paris and buy their couture clothes, and then they just keep them in a trunk for a year, so they wouldn’t be so new when they were worn for the first time. It has a lot to do with the idea that the sort of shiny newness of fashion may seem a little bit fashion victim-y. They weren’t having to show off that it was brand new.”.

In a recent development, in case there was any doubt that the distressed effect is just another example of insular runway fashion, people are actually buying ripped, stained, destroyed clothes outside of the designer space, too. Just look at Distressed Fest, a biannual, bicoastal vintage clothing pop-up event focused on heavily worn, threadbare, and destroyed garments that are sold for a premium. Scuffs, rips, stains, and all: as ironic as it may be, fashion’s current status symbol now is looking like you’ve been through something.

In a recent development, depending on who you are, cooking a full Thanksgiving dinner can bring either excitement or complete dread. If you fall into the latter camp, Costco is here to help with its newest offering in the deli department.

In a recent development, laura Lamb of @costcohotfinds shared on social media that the warehouse’s Thanksgiving dinner kit has officially returned for 2026. The prepared meal includes all the holiday essentials, with much of the prep work already taken care of.

Each kit comes with a seasoned half turkey breast over a bed of herbed stuffing, along with Yukon Gold mashed potatoes, green beans, cranberry sauce, and gravy. Costco is pricing the meal at just $3.99 per pound, which works out to around $40 to feed seven to eight people.

The label includes simple instructions for preparing all the components. The uncooked turkey, naturally, takes the most time. Since it’s placed over the stuffing, the turkey drippings add even more flavor and moisture as it roasts in the oven.

It has been revealed that the warehouse keeps this dinner kit pretty consistent from year to year, although one Costco shopper wasn’t as impressed with a particular component this time around. Costco fan and content creator @photogami reports that the gravy is a bit underseasoned and not as good as it was last year. (Thankfully, this glitch has a pretty easy solution.).

Lamb also noted that you’ll still need to buy a few extras to round out the meal, like dinner rolls and pumpkin pie. And if you’re a stuffing lover, the amount that comes in Costco’s kit might not be enough for you.

Still, it’s hard to argue with the price and convenience—and members are already eager to pick up a kit for their own holiday celebrations. “Got this last year and it was all absolutely delicious,” one user on Instagram wrote. “Highly recommend.” Another commented, “This is such a great idea for a smaller Thanksgiving!”.

Industry observers note that if you want to grab a kit for yourself, initiative accordingly. All Costco locations are closed on Thanksgiving Day, so you only have a few days to snag one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I’m tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients. With 26 grams of protein and just 25 minutes of prep-and-cook time, HelloFresh’s Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl is a great solution for dinner.

According to recent reports, this flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

You’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

It has been revealed that true to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how promptly they pinked up.

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

This is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

Would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover upcoming flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table quickly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.

Industry News: Kim and Khloé Kardashian’s Beauty Trip Didn’t Quite Go to Plan—Here’s What to Know Before Booking Yours

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between the salmon sperm facials, the skin boosters, and the next generation of lasers, there’s plenty to pique the interest of the beauty obsessive in South Korea.
  • On Wednesday’s episode of her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land, Koko and her close friend La La Anthony reminisced about their August 2025 trip to South Korea, where they enthusiastically availed themselves of the country’s advanced cosmetic treatments—with some less-than-desirable results.
  • “Kim and I came back deformed, you came back beautiful and the plane ride just made it so much worse,” Kardashian told Anthony, recalling how their post-treatment appearances had kept them holed up in their hotel room.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between the salmon sperm facials, the skin boosters, and the next generation of lasers, there’s plenty to pique the interest of the beauty obsessive in South Korea. So much so that vacations are increasingly being organized around visits to the dermatologist’s office. But how much is too much when it comes to our beauty itineraries? Just ask Khloé and Kim Kardashian.

On Wednesday’s episode of her podcast, Khloé in Wonder Land, Koko and her close friend La La Anthony reminisced about their August 2025 trip to South Korea, where they enthusiastically availed themselves of the country’s advanced cosmetic treatments—with some less-than-desirable results.

“Kim and I came back deformed, you came back beautiful and the plane ride just made it so much worse,” Kardashian told Anthony, recalling how their post-treatment appearances had kept them holed up in their hotel room.

Industry observers note that the Kardashians are, of course, well-versed in the world of aesthetics. Over the years, the sisters have been particularly candid about their experiments with everything from the vampire facial to regenerative skin treatments. But even for those with the world’s most sought-after dermatologists on speed dial, things don’t always go to plan.

While it’s unclear precisely which procedures the sisters underwent—photos shared on Kim’s Instagram at the time indicated her receiving facial treatments and an IV infusion—their experience raises some pertinent questions. How much research should we be doing before traveling abroad for cosmetic treatments? How many procedures can we feasibly—and safely—fit into a vacation? And how do we know when something has actually gone wrong?

Industry observers note that the lure of a beauty vacation is understandable. South Korea, in particular, is at the forefront of aesthetic innovation, with technologies and treatments that aren’t yet widely available in the United States. And as our collective beauty literacy has expanded, so too has our appetite for more technologically sophisticated treatments. A facial no longer necessarily means an hour of extractions and massage. But there is a distinction to be made between a beauty treatment and a medical procedure. Just because something is marketed as minimally invasive, or requires no incisions, doesn’t mean it is without risk. Nor does its ubiquity on TikTok necessarily speak to its suitability for your own skin.

Industry observers note that “Traveling for treatment isn't the same as having unsafe treatment,” says consultant dermatologist Dr. Sidra Khan. “What travel adds is complexity: a different regulatory system, possibly a language barrier, often a compressed consultation, and being thousands of miles from your practitioner during recovery.”.

“A beautiful clinic, an impressive Instagram following and a gallery of celebrity clients don’t really tell you much about the practitioner’s medical credentials or what results you might expect,” adds cosmetic surgeon and aesthetics specialist Dr. Paul Banwell. Independently verify your practitioner’s qualifications and registration with the relevant medical regulator, and establish whether the clinic is equipped to manage complications. Khan recommends arranging a virtual consultation with the treating doctor before booking anything, and asking about their experience with your particular skin tone, the products and devices they intend to use, and why. “A holiday itinerary shouldn't replace informed consent.”.

For London-based aesthetics and NHS doctor Dr. Alicia Gonzalez-Fernandez, the marketing of medical procedures as vacation packages is itself a red flag. “On a handful of occasions, I have encountered patients that have come into A&E straight from the airport,” she notes of her experiences working in emergency medicine. She cautions against practitioners who pressure patients into additional procedures or fail to adequately discuss complications and aftercare. “We are not in the business of making people self-conscious about things that are not a problem for them.”.

Then there’s the phenomenon of “treatment stacking.” While certain procedures can complement one another, squeezing several into a short period of time can increase the likelihood of complications. “Many of these treatments work by creating a controlled injury that the skin then repairs, and doing several close together doesn't give it time to recover,” explains aesthetics doctor Dr. Priya Verma. “That raises the risk of prolonged inflammation, infection and pigmentation changes, particularly in darker skin tones.”.

In a recent development, multiple procedures can also make it harder to establish which treatment is responsible for an adverse reaction, notes aesthetics doctor Dr. Ahmed El Muntasar. “Ultimately, I’d much rather a patient’s treatment schedule was dictated by how their skin is recovering than by the date of their flight home.”.

Consider, too, how conducive the rest of your vacation itinerary is to your skin’s recovery. As Verma notes, the low humidity in airplane cabins can exacerbate dryness and sensitivity in already compromised skin, while sun exposure can increase the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. There is no universal rule about how soon you can fly after a non-surgical cosmetic procedure, says Khan, but you should allow ample time for recovery and an in-person review before your departure. (With surgical procedures, flying also carries an increased risk of blood clots, making a conversation with your surgeon about your travel plans particularly important.).

According to recent reports, there's also the question of downtime. An unfortunate-looking reflection in the hotel bathroom mirror doesn’t necessarily mean a treatment has been “botched.” Verma makes an important distinction: “Downtime is the expected redness, swelling or flaking that settles over a few days. Dissatisfaction is when the skin has healed but you're not happy with the result. A complication is a medical problem that needs treating.”.

Knowing what to expect—and for how long—is something to establish with your practitioner well before the treatment itself. The trajectory of your recovery is key: Increasing pain, spreading redness, heat, discharge, or fever warrant prompt medical attention.

There are, however, symptoms that warrant immediate medical attention. Following dermal filler injections, for example, the FDA advises seeking immediate medical care for unusual pain, changes to your vision, white, gray, or blue discoloration around the injection site, or signs of a stroke. These may indicate that the blood supply has been compromised.

“If there are red-flag symptoms, don't just get on a plane because you'd rather deal with it at home,” stresses Khan. “Some complications are time-critical, so get seen locally.”.

In a recent development, in non-emergency situations, contact your original practitioner for an in-person review and document your recovery with photographs taken in consistent lighting. El Muntasar recommends obtaining your full treatment records, including the names, quantities, and batch numbers of any injectables, or the device and settings used for laser treatments. Seek an independent medical opinion from someone experienced in managing complications if you remain concerned.

According to recent reports, as distressing as it can be to feel unhappy with your appearance, resist the temptation to immediately book another aesthetic procedure. “Swelling can make certain areas appear overfilled or disproportionate, and adding more filler to try to balance things out can leave a patient with an entirely different problem once that swelling subsides,” explains Banwell.

“More treatment isn’t always the antidote to treatment,” says Khan. Anti-wrinkle injections can take around two weeks to reach their full effect, filler can take several weeks to settle, and collagen remodeling following laser treatments or microneedling continues for months. The same caution applies to overzealous at-home skincare. “Your freshly lasered face is not the moment to try the acids and retinoids you picked up at duty-free.”.

According to recent reports, and while you might have meticulously mapped out your Seoul shopping itinerary, restaurant reservations, and dermatology appointments, have you given quite as much thought to what happens when you get home? Establishing a proposal for follow-up care, obtaining a record of your procedures, and checking whether your insurance covers complications should all factor into the planning process. El Muntasar recommends getting your aftercare plan in writing, including details of who you can contact outside of clinic hours and who is responsible for any additional medical expenses should you need to extend your stay.

It has been revealed that by all means, indulge your K-beauty curiosity. Just make sure you’re approaching your dermatological appointments with a little more discernment than your haul at Olive Young.

Breaking: Gravy-Braised Turkey

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that cooking a whole turkey is a commitment.
  • According to recent reports, this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

According to recent reports, this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first vital step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

Recent findings suggest that add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Sources indicate that let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman indicates. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, says of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

What Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the upcoming podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

Industry observers note that the Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this new outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman indicates. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”.

According to recent reports, at Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she states.

In a recent development, the vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she notes. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up rapidly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Industry observers note that alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.
