📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “There is and will always be only one Veruschka,” Richard Avedon wrote in the May 1972 concern of Vogue in an impassioned tribute to his muse. More than half a century later, his words still ring true. Since news broke of the German supermodel’s death at the age of 87, generations of fashion’s image-makers, designers, and models have been reflecting on her immeasurable influence.

In a recent development, A protagonist of some of the most fantastical fashion editorials ever committed to the pages of Vogue and a prolific cover star, Veruschka helped expand the possibilities of what a model could be. Her body was her artistic medium, her imagination as instrumental to the making of a photograph as that of the person behind the lens. Her creative curiosity would endure long after her heyday in the 1960s and ’70s, finding expression in her experiments with body painting and camouflage, her performance art, and her occasional, much-feted returns to the runway.

According to recent reports, for those who knew and worked with Veruschka, though, there was as much to marvel at away from the camera: her generosity of spirit, quiet eccentricities, intellectual curiosity, and her sense of humor. In the tributes shared with Vogue below, fellow models recall their first encounters with a woman whose photographs once adorned their bedroom walls, while designers and photographers reflect on the creative communion they shared with her—and how rare a model like Veruschka is today.

I am so sad to hear the news of Veruschka’s passing. When I started modeling in 1966, she was one of my idols—she was so beautiful and exotic. I had always wanted to meet her, and then in the 1980s, while I was appearing on Broadway in the musical My One and Only, a knock came on my dressing room door after the performance. I opened it and, to my surprise and huge delight, Veruschka was standing there. It was so lovely to finally meet her, and she was absolutely divine, and we chatted for ages. She certainly is one of the greatest of all models. RIP, beautiful lady.

In a recent development, veruschka was an extraordinary artist that I was blessed to know. Thank you, Vera….

According to recent reports, I remember sitting in the library at Saint Martins, transfixed by the camouflage photographs in Veruschka: Trans-Figurations, the book she made with Holger Trülzsch. Years later, when I had the chance to work with her, I knew I wanted her to close my spring/summer 2011 show. We flew her in from Berlin and made her a bespoke dress for the finale. What I loved about working with her was how open she was to the ideas behind the collection and how wholeheartedly she embraced them. She was 71 and absolutely majestic on the runway. She had a presence unlike anyone else. A creative powerhouse and a true original.

According to recent reports, being a model is an art form, and she was one of the people who truly mastered it. She had both creativity and respect for what she was doing. When we worked with her, she was incredibly impressive. There was an energy, a grace, and a lasting presence that you don’t see so often today. The lifespan of a model’s career seems to have become so much shorter. I sometimes wonder if, in the way the industry works today, we’re leaving less room for someone to become truly iconic.

Sources indicate that when I was a young girl, my bedroom walls were covered in photographs of Veruschka. To me, she looked like she had stepped out of another world—a dream I looked up to, one of the incredible women who had paved the way before me. I used to lie in bed, staring at those pictures, wondering what it would be like actually to know someone like her. Years later, that dream literally knocked on my door.

We ended up living together at our agent Zoli’s house on East 63rd Street. For months, after a long day’s work, we would settle in for the evening with our sketchbooks. I can still see her drawing her little cats—curled up, stretching out, or peeking from the corners of the pages—while I sketched beside her. We didn’t need to say much; the quiet between us always felt so full.

Veruschka was always an enigma to me, a woman with a poetic soul and a nature I could never quite put a name to. She had a wicked little smile and a twinkle in her eye when she’d look up from her drawing, as if she knew a secret about the world she might someday share. Her voice was low and sensuous, and she was always kinder than anyone needed to be.

In a recent development, sometimes, while watching her sketch, I would think back to that little girl staring at the pictures on her wall. I wished I could tell her that one day she would be sitting right beside her icon, and that Veruschka would be her friend. I have always loved Veruschka, and I always will. Knowing she taught me that dreams really do come true. She was mine.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Boasting a brief ingredient list and a short cooking time, this easy chicken dish is one you’ll be making all season.
  • Industry observers note that the protein:You don’t have to limit yourself to chicken here.
  • The crunch:The sage leaves crisp while the butter browns, but there are also ways to add more texture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Boasting a brief ingredient list and a short cooking time, this easy chicken dish is one you’ll be making all season. Basic butter becomes the star here—it turns brown and nutty, then gets infused with sage and garlic for a savory sauce that’s basted over simply seasoned chicken breasts. A substantial squeeze of lemon, plus its zest, helps balance the richness. This skillet dinner is perfect for a speedy weeknight meal, but it’s also special enough for manufacturer.

Industry observers note that the protein:You don’t have to limit yourself to chicken here. Feel free to replace the breasts with pork chops, shrimp, scallops, or skinless salmon or halibut fillets. Simply adjust the cooking time to properly cook the protein, but be sure to maintain a medium heat. While meat and fish are often cooked on medium-high heat for a nice char, it needs to be a bit lower to avoid bitter residue in the pan, since the butter will be browned immediately afterward.

The crunch:The sage leaves crisp while the butter browns, but there are also ways to add more texture. Stirring in a handful of slivered almonds toward the end of cooking adds to the nuttiness of the dish; pine nuts, pistachios, or roughly chopped walnuts would also work. If you have a container of them, feel free to sprinkle some fried onions on top tableside.

Storage and serving ideas:This is not a make-ahead situation; it should be eaten immediately after it’s cooked. Serve with a simple salad dressed in a light vinaigrette to balance the richness. To soak up the sauce, mashed potatoes—traditional or sweet—are ideal. Or, to add another nutty element, roast some Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, or butternut squash to eat alongside and round out the meal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Sources indicate that place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

Sources indicate that while the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

Industry News: The Body and The Teen Drama Fashion Machine

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Body, Overcompensating, Off Campus… Just when you thought pop culture had reached peak teen drama, the streaming giants release another slew of bingeable reveals to capture the hearts of Gen Z and Gen Alpha viewers, and newly introduced audiences for their sponsors.
  • Sources indicate that taking the lion’s share of views at the moment is The Body, a coming-of-age psychodrama set in a Catholic school, which has quickly made its way into fashion fans’ For You pages.
  • Costumed by Mirren Gordon-Crozier, the series features iconic ‘00s designs, including the Dior Saddle bag, a Louis Vuitton x Takashi Murakami Pochette, a John Galliano-era “J’adore Dior” T-shirt, and various Juicy Couture accessories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Body, Overcompensating, Off Campus… Just when you thought pop culture had reached peak teen drama, the streaming giants release another slew of bingeable reveals to capture the hearts of Gen Z and Gen Alpha viewers, and newly introduced audiences for their sponsors.

Sources indicate that taking the lion’s share of views at the moment is The Body, a coming-of-age psychodrama set in a Catholic school, which has quickly made its way into fashion fans’ For You pages. Just this week, the Netflix show has amassed 9.5 million views, marking its second week in the platform’s global top 10. It’s also right now the number one show in 39 countries.

Costumed by Mirren Gordon-Crozier, the series features iconic ‘00s designs, including the Dior Saddle bag, a Louis Vuitton x Takashi Murakami Pochette, a John Galliano-era “J’adore Dior” T-shirt, and various Juicy Couture accessories.

Fans have responded online, applauding the depth and details of the costuming. “This is why the Y2K clothing in The Body was so accurate,” reads one TikTok with 106,200 views. Another TikTok splices glamorous scenes from the series, showing massive sunglasses, velour tracksuits and flip-flops, soundtracked to Gwen Stefani’s 2004 hit, “Rich Girl” (257,000 views).

“With a show set in 2004, the pieces had to feel real — not like a costume of the era,” says Gordon-Crozier, recalling that a lot was sourced vintage and last-minute finds in local Toronto thrift shops. “The ‘J’adore Dior’, the Juicy, the City bag, and the Murakami were the status language of those girls.” Since the show aired, Gordon-Crozier has received hundreds of messages on Instagram asking where pieces are from, along with compliments on the styling. “Y2K fashion was loud, optimistic and completely unembarrassed,” she says. “It was pre-Instagram, so there was no algorithm telling you what to wear.”.

True to the period, Gordon-Crozier even recreated tabloid clapback tees, including ‘Team Aniston’ and ‘Team Jolie’ tees for the identical twins Bailey and Britt Bradley. “That generation grew up on new, flashy pop stars like Britney Spears, Paris Hilton and Christina Aguilera, who were all about excess and fun,” she adds. “Today, there’s so much curation. Quiet luxury I’m sure is a response to that in a way.”.

It has been revealed that “Teen dramas have become Gen Z’s lookbook,” indicates Rick Jackson, marketing agency Pion’s head of B2B content. “Unlike a traditional ad, a show places a product inside a character, and a lifestyle young people already aspire to.” As such, the City bag or the Juicy Couture tracksuit isn’t just shown, but lived, he explains. “Because Gen Z watches with their phone in hand, an outfit can go from screen to TikTok to checkout within hours,” he adds. This is a substantial draw for brands, and arguably a far stronger marker of credibility than paid media.

Balenciaga’s City bags were sourced especially for the The Body.

Many brands are wise to this already. H&M consistently ties its collections to Netflix youth hits, channeling the mood of each series into capsules: ’80s retro for Stranger Things, romcom prep for To All the Boys and bold retro looks for Sex Education. This consistency is key. Based on Pion’s recent report into Gen Zalpha (16-24-year-olds), cultural relevance needs ongoing presence in youth culture — on screen, through sport, music and movements — instead of a single, one-off moment.

It has been revealed that “Placement gives brands cultural relevance with a generation that’s sceptical of traditional advertising,” says William Weeks, Pion’s chief marketing officer. On the primary market, he explains, interest converts fastest when there’s an accessible entry point. That might mean a discount, a dupe-friendly price point, or a smaller item from the brand. Merch can also fill this gap.

But resale will reap the rewards first, experts agree. Luxury pieces can generate traction as resale offers young fans a way to tap into the moment at a fraction of the price. “For brands, these series are less about a direct ‘buy this exact item’ moment and more about spotting cultural momentum early,” indicates Sophy Vanner, a strategy partner at creative agency Amplify. “Often, secondary platforms get the first wave of demand because fans want the hunt and the specific reference point.”.

According to recent reports, “The smartest brands play both,” says Weeks. “They win the cultural moment on screen and make it affordable for young fans to buy into straight away.”.

Vanner argues that another way primary brands can still win is by leaning into the codes, lore and IRL spaces around those moments: “Turning on-screen energy into real-world hangouts, collabs and shared rituals rather than just another product push.”.

According to recent reports, euphoria has served as the playbook here, offering everything from pop-ups where guests can have their makeup done, DJ-ed events and talks. In 2022, A24 also debuted a makeup line with Euphoria's makeup artist Donni Davy called Half Magic. Globally, the number of TikTok videos posted using #EuphoriaMakeup increased by 1,051% year on year between November 2025 and October 2026, TikTok shares with Vogue Business.

The Half Magic brand was founded by A24 and Euphoria makeup artist Donni Davy.

In February next year, Amazon will air the second season of Benito Skinner’s Overcompensating, a comedy about a closeted ex-footballer. The show has quickly become known for its very 2010s costumes. Already, the first season (aired in 2025) has built a cult following around its preppy fare. Mall prep brands such as J.Crew, Polo Ralph Lauren, and even L.L.Bean have become associated with the male characters.

Recent findings suggest that “We were trying to tap into archetypal ways that people represent themselves — the way that kids try to fit in by overdressing in the version of the thing that they want to be,” indicates the show’s costume designer Hanna Puley. “For the girls it was a lot of fast fashion. I think we pulled a fair bit from H&M and stuff that was readily accessible and felt familiar. It’s that Forever 21 aesthetic.”.

It has been revealed that the costuming tracks with a shift that’s been underway for a while among young consumers. Mall brands are having a comeback, accessible luxury is performing (Ralph Lauren revenues climbed 10% in the last quarter), and nostalgic pre-loved designer accessories continue to captivate. It’s exactly why brands should look to these love-triangle, first-kiss dramas to position themselves in the zeitgeist.

In a recent development, consider also Amazon’s Off Campus, which launched in May and follows a men’s ice hockey team in their heterosexual dalliances. Aside from the usual plot analyses that flood TikTok, the show has also built a strong online contingent of fans wanting to discuss the outfits. Leading female protagonist Allie Hayes, played by Mika Abdalla, appeared in one episode wearing a recreation of Jennifer Lopez’s Donatella Versace-designed dress for Halloween. The piece went viral on TikTok, with creators sharing behind-the-scenes footage of costume designer Charlene Akuamoah at work and, of course, their own reactions. One video shared generated 258,200 views.

According to recent reports, “I think part of what makes Off Campus resonate so strongly from a fashion perspective is that the clothing strikes a balance between aspiration and relatability,” states Akuamoah. “I was intentional about mixing contemporary brands, vintage pieces, and different price points to create wardrobes that felt authentic to each character. Younger audiences are increasingly turning to television for fashion inspiration, and social media allows them to immediately identify, share and shop what they see on screen.”.

Off Campus star Ella Bright attends the Miu Miu Womenswear Spring/Summer 2027 show.

Across the board, the teen drama genre remains a well for fashion inspiration. Past contenders include US first-love hit, The Summer I Turned Pretty, Spanish private-school thriller Elite and A24’s Euphoria. With them come merch opportunities for the streaming platform and commercial careers for actors beyond the big screen. A24 is no stranger to merch, and after Euphoria, starring actresses Zendaya and Sydney Sweeney have both gone on to become style icons in their own right, closely followed for their press tour wardrobes and brand ambassadorships with Louis Vuitton and Miu Miu, respectively.

It has been revealed that “These shows used to be about putting products on screen, but today the real value sits with the cast themselves,” says Alison Bringé, Launchmetrics’s chief marketing officer. She points to the average media impact value (MIV) of an Instagram post from some of The Summer I Turned Pretty’s leading stars: Lola Tung ($387,000), Christopher Briney ($256,000) and Gavin Casalegno ($354,000). “Their fandoms don’t just watch: they follow, recreate and share, which turns these actors into commercial voices with real staying power,” Bringé adds. “That’s why we’re seeing brands sign them as ambassadors rather than treating them as a one-season moment.”.

Similarly, Ella Bright, an Off Campus star, commands an MIV of $757,000 per Instagram post. Selena Gomez’s Rare Beauty also declared Bright as its first-ever brand ambassador in July. The news culminated in a MIV of $4.6 million within a week and lifted the brand’s overall performance by over 138% the same day, with the top post driving $815,000 in MIV alone. In September, Belmont Cameli, another star from the series, generated $943,000 in MIV in one week for Saint Laurent through a single post.

Devin Barrett, General Idea’s copy director for social and culture, says that teen dramas offer brands a direct link to vibrant cultural conversations and the opportunity to align with future breakout talent. He points to The Body as a fictional portrait of the affluent 2004 teen consumer, explaining that it proffers a new style inspiration source beyond the oversaturated ’00s paparazzi imagery. “Highlights like this bring Gen Z and Gen Alpha into an era they didn’t originally experience, orchestrating a richer world around Y2K aesthetics,” he says. “It unlocks the potential for new brand ambassadors with an authentic connection to products like the Dior Saddle bag.”.

Of course, fashion has long been a fan of teen dramas, both on television and in the movies. Millennials and Gen-Xers might remember Grease, The Breakfast Club and Mean Girls as historic style inspirations. Demonstrates, however, offer a more enduring marketing avenue for brands to tap into throughout a storyline. “These shows freeze a fleeting, perfect moment — the first love, a friendship group that feels like the whole world,” says Katy Lubin, Lyst’s VP of brand and communications. “The characters are flawed and human. For a brand, being part of that feels genuine in a way a campaign shoot just can’t.” As she sees it, specific pieces become associated with specific character traits, much like the Fendi Baguette gave a cool, Fresh York yuppie association through Sex and the City’s Carrie Bradshaw.

Benito Skinner, director and lead in Overcompensating, attends the Burberry Spring/Summer 2027 show.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, because viewers follow demonstrates for long periods across seasons, it means the fashion choices can also shift and evolve, presenting new opportunities for brands. Competitors will need to be agile. Indeed, next season, Overcompensating is leaning into a different vibe, Puley tells Vogue Business. She’s interested to see how viewers react. “We’re not veering so mainstream. There’s a lot more niche stuff,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve been there, excited to join your family for Thanksgiving dinner, only to realize that even the green bean casserole isn’t just veggies. This time, though, you can enjoy the creamiest green bean casserole without the dairy or meat. For the ultimate creamy bite, we make a DIY vegan version of condensed cream of mushroom soup with fresh mushrooms, shallots, and almond milk. We're also super into the onion topping on this casserole—it's broiled in the oven with a touch of oil but so much more fragrant and vibrant in flavor than the fried ones that come in a can.

It has been revealed that looking for more vegan Thanksgiving sides? Check out our vegan mashed potatoes! They're loaded with rosemary and garlic. SO. GOOD.

It has been revealed that preheat oven to medium broil and line a medium baking sheet with aluminum foil. In a medium bowl, toss onion with olive oil and season with salt and pepper. Add flour and Panko and toss until the onions are coated. Broil, tossing every 2 to 3 minutes, until onions are crisp and golden, about 6 to 8 minutes total. Turn oven down to 375°.

Prepare an ice bath. In a large pot of heavily salted boiling water, add green beans and cook until bright green, 3 to 4 minutes. Using a slotted spoon or tongs, promptly transfer green beans to the ice bath to cool. Drain and transfer to a large bowl.

In a recent development, in a large skillet over medium heat, heat 2 tablespoons olive oil. Add shallots and cook, stirring occasionally, until tender, about 5 minutes. Add mushrooms and season with salt and pepper. Cook, stirring often, until mushrooms are golden, about 5 minutes more. Stir in garlic, then transfer the mixture to the bowl with the green beans.

Heat the remaining 4 tablespoons of olive oil in the same skillet over medium heat. Whisk in flour and cook until golden, about 2 minutes. Gradually whisk in almond milk and bring to a simmer.

Cook until thickened, about 4 minutes. Remove from heat and season to taste with salt and pepper.

Add the green bean mixture and toss until everything is evenly combined.

Recent findings suggest that transfer the mixture to a medium casserole dish. Bake until warmed through and bubbling around the edges, about 20 minutes. Top with the "fried" onions and bake for 5 minutes more.

Industry observers note that if you’re not into creamy, melty macaroni and cheese with an insanely satisfying cheese-pull, then you might want to find another mac recipe. Sorry, but this slow-cooker macaroni and cheese is just too darn dreamy.

Industry observers note that would Grandma really be all that upset if you tried a latest stuffing this holiday? Her cornbread stuffing is undoubtedly delicious and nostalgic, but what if we switched it up a bit this year and tried something new? Enter: flaky, savory-sweet croissant stuffing.

Onion Soup Mix Roasted Potatoes.

Charred Cabbage With Yogurt and Hot Sauce

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp.
  • In a recent development, preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind. Charred aggressively, it takes on a smoky, almost meaty quality—it’s the main event. A drizzle of hot sauce, crispy breadcrumbs, and a cooling yogurt sauce round it out. Treat cabbage like a protein, and it will reward you.

More showstopping cabbage recipes here.

In a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp. brine, 1 small shallot, roughly chopped, 3 garlic cloves, 3 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, juice of 1 navel orange, and 1 tsp. kosher salt. Blend on high, taking a pause to scrape the sides, until smooth. With the blender running on low, slowly pour in 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil until the sauce is silky and runny. Transfer the sauce to a bottle or jar and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

In a recent development, preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven. Line a sheet tray with parchment paper.

It has been revealed that make the Cabbage: Cut 1 large head green cabbage in half, then slice each half into four wedges. Arrange on the prepared sheet tray, drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil and kosher salt, and massage it into all those craggy layers. Roast on the center rack for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Set the broiler to high and slide the cabbage to the top rack. Broil for 2–4 minutes, until the edges are deeply charred and irresistibly crispy.

While the Cabbage Roasts, Make the Breadcrumbs: In a small skillet over medium heat, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter with 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Stir in ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 1 garlic clove, finely grated, and ½ tsp. kosher salt, then toast, stirring constantly, until golden and fragrant. Remove from the heat and mix in ¼ preserved lemon, store-bought or homemade, peel only, finely diced, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, and 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley. Set aside to cool.

Make the Yogurt: In a small bowl, whisk together 1 cup full-fat Greek yogurt or labne, zest and juice ½ lemon, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, and 1 tsp. kosher salt until smooth and creamy.

It has been revealed that when the cabbage is ready, swoop the yogurt across a serving plate. Arrange the cabbage wedges at dramatic angles. Drizzle generously with hot sauce, letting it seep into the leaves. Finish with the golden breadcrumbs, fresh dill fronds, and a few extra grates of lemon zest. Serve immediately.

BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero.
  • While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work.
  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

It has been revealed that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

How Costume Designer Trish Summerville Reimagined ’70s Hollywood Style for ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood is rich in striking, darkly memorable imagery: Margot Robbie shimmying in a sunshine-yellow two-piece at the Playboy Mansion; the sunbaked menace of Brad Pitt’s visit to the Manson ranch; the audaciously bloody denouement, all pit bulls and flamethrowers, playing out high in the Hollywood Hills, with the glittering carpet of nighttime Los Angeles extending endlessly beyond.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood is rich in striking, darkly memorable imagery: Margot Robbie shimmying in a sunshine-yellow two-piece at the Playboy Mansion; the sunbaked menace of Brad Pitt’s visit to the Manson ranch; the audaciously bloody denouement, all pit bulls and flamethrowers, playing out high in the Hollywood Hills, with the glittering carpet of nighttime Los Angeles extending endlessly beyond.

Industry observers note that but for some—this writer included—the film’s most indelible legacy is its costumes. And, more specifically, those of Pitt’s laid-back (and possibly wife-murdering) stuntman Cliff Booth. Double-denim layers, gold-rimmed aviators, scuffed moccasins—and, of course, those Hawaiian shirts—the character’s late-’60s California cool burnt up the screen and almost certainly played a part in the Americana wave that plenty of menswear fanatics are still riding.

Industry observers note that so, when David Fincher stepped into the director’s chair for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth—the Netflix film picks up the story of Pitt’s character nearly a decade later—the task of evolving those indelible looks fell to one of the director’s most trusted creative collaborators: costume designer Trish Summerville. Indeed, the trust ran so deep (the pair had previously worked together on The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, Gone Girl, and Mank) that Summerville didn’t even know what the project was when she stated yes. “I’m always in for whatever he’s doing,” she tells Vogue. “I don’t know anyone else I would do that with.”.

Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth, Elizabeth Debicki as Karen Crosby, Scott Caan as Charlie Peters, and Carla Gugino as Toni Becka.

Sources indicate that across the eight-year gap between the two films, a lot has changed in Hollywood—not least in its style. By the late ’70s, it’s the heady era of Studio 54 excess, punk-rock rebellion, and Halston halter necks. Still, rather than leaning into disco-fever, polyester-everything clichés, Summerville looked to the real-world period artifacts she could get her hands on locally, scouring the vintage mail-order catalogs and archival racks at Los Angeles’s legendary Western Costume, among other places. Under Fincher’s famously exacting eye, every garment had to serve the story without ever feeling like, well, a costume—and it was a challenge that required building nearly every piece from the ground up. (Though with a little inspiration from some select vintage garments along the way.).

According to recent reports, arguably most seductive of all are the costumes worn by Elizabeth Debicki: in Cliff Booth, the six-foot-three Australian actor plays Karen Crosby, an enigmatic, glamorous Hollywood studio executive whose crisp wardrobe practically gleams within the seedy underbelly of 1970s Los Angeles conjured by the film’s production designer, Donald Graham Burt. Dressed exclusively in varying shades of white—a strict mandate from Fincher that required extensive color-testing with cinematographer Eric Messerschmidt—Debicki’s looks deliberately stand out, but never feel disconnected from the world around her.

Sources indicate that “Unless it’s something in the script that really wants the clothing and the costumes to jump off the screen, I never want it to distract,” Summerville indicates, a sentiment that could apply to the lived-in textures of her costuming work on Cliff Booth as a whole. “It should just help you watch this story.”.

Below, Summerville talks figuring out exactly the right cut of 1970s denim for Pitt, looking to Lauren Hutton and Cher as muses for Debicki, and why the decade’s unstudied sex appeal continues to shape fashion today.

Vogue: Obviously, you’ve worked with David a number of times before—but how did this project end up in your lap?

Trish Summerville: It came up through Ceán Chaffin, who’s Dave’s producer. We met at a coffee shop, which was very formal for us, and she didn’t really say what it was—she just said that they had a project coming up, a film, and they’d like me to do it, but she couldn’t tell me what it was because it was quite secretive at that time.

It has been revealed that I had to say I was in without knowing what it was. Because of my history with Dave and really liking working with him a lot, I’m always in for whatever he’s doing. I always hope I’m available when he has a project; I hope I’m asked to do it. The only thing I knew was it was a film and it would be in LA, and that was all I knew until I agreed. And then I got an explanation of what it was, and a text from Dave afterwards saying, “Yay, I’m glad you’re in.”.

I presume you had seen the first film. Did you revisit it before starting work?

Yeah, I definitely had seen the first film, and after they did call me, I did rewatch it so I could get refamiliarized with the characters, but then I got the script, and realized there’s not a lot of overlap in the characters—it’s pretty much just Brad, so it’s a whole new story about him.

When we last saw Cliff Booth, it was 1969, and this film is set 1977. How did you first start thinking about the ways in which his look—and the look of the city generally—was going to feel distinct from the first film?

Recent findings suggest that I did a lot of research. We have a couple of rental houses here that have pretty extensive research materials, and Western Costume is always a great place to start. They have a search library of periodicals, photographs from sets, behind-the-scenes stuff, and every kind of catalog you could imagine. So it was really important for me to look at everything from films in Hollywood that were happening, behind the scenes, the actors, and then also looking at everyday catalogs like JCPenney or Sears catalogs, looking at Vogue magazine, Ebony magazine—just so I could have a range. It needed to cover what’s depicted on screen as the movie within the movie, then also, how people dressed every day.

Even though there wasn’t fast fashion like there is now, in that amount of time you did see a shift in silhouettes across both men’s and women’s clothing—shapes of jeans, shapes of jackets, the jewelry. But with Brad’s character, it was really about keeping the integrity of who his character is, and the ease—Cliff Booth is really just a fucking cool guy. It was about shifting him a little bit: changing the silhouette of his jeans, giving him Roper suede boots instead of moccasins, not doing as many layers this time, having his shirts buttoned a little bit lower. He’s really, really comfortable with who he is.

Oh, and we definitely wanted to start the film off with the Hawaiian shirt from the first film, so the audience has something to immediately recognize and feel a kinship with.

According to recent reports, tarantino is known for having quite detailed descriptions in his scripts about costumes. Was that the case here?

It has been revealed that yeah, in some instances there were. Some of the descriptions of Cliff, it would say he’s wearing Billy Jack boots, or that he puts on puka shells for when he tends bar. But it wasn’t excessive. We stuck pretty much to anything that was a key story point, or that seemed really integral to the character—he’d maybe describe that he’s wearing sunglasses here, or a leather jacket. With Hot Rod, it would describe the style of clothing he would wear, but nothing as specific as a color or anything like that.

How much of the costumes were sourced, recreated, or made from scratch?

In a recent development, pretty much most of it was made, at least for our principals. When it’s a period film, and you have stunts, and a really long shoot—we shot, I think it was 105 or 107 days—you really have to have at least doubles of things. It’s too scary. We kind of have a saying in the costume world: “If you have one, you have none.” For Elizabeth, we made her costumes, especially because Dave was very specific that he just wanted her always in a tone of white, and white is very scary in general.

Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth and Elizabeth Debicki as Karen Crosby.

Recent findings suggest that and with Brad’s character, even the shirts that we found for him—like the Hawaiian shirt and the tiki shirts and the liquor bottle shirt—we bought rayon fabric and printed all those ourselves. For the liquor bottle shirt, one of my shoppers found a vintage one and sent me a picture, and I was like, “Oh my God, that shirt is amazing.” Then I found another one, and then one of the guys in our department said, “Wait, I think I have this shirt at home—I’ve had it for 20 or 30 years.” So we found three different versions of that shirt from the mid-to-late ’40s to the ’70s. I selected all the bottles I liked from the different shirts and changed the colors a bit, and the illustrator I work with drew up a pattern, and then we had a printer here in Los Angeles print up the fabric. We even built jeans for him—we found a Levi’s shape that was great on him, and then we built multiples of them. His barong—the shirt he wears at the end—we ended up making 68 of that particular shirt. It’s all embroidered, all natural fibers, because of how the shirt is used for him and his stunt guy.

It has been revealed that brad knows a lot about fashion—he has his own cashmere line, for one. Was dressing him quite a collaborative process?

According to recent reports, it is. He does have opinions, and he’ll bring in inspiration pieces or things that he likes. Then it’s just trying a bunch of shapes, and retrying things once we build them. He really liked the idea of having T-shirts that leaned into an automotive inspiration for Cliff, which makes sense, and we chose to use that at the speedway in the figure-eight races. Working with the Evel Knievel logo, because Evel Knievel was so substantial at that time, and being a stuntman, he would really have an affinity for that. And then Brad was like, “Oh, I want a red, white, and blue helmet.” So we went to the props guy and said, “We’re going to have this Evel Knievel vibe for him for the T-shirts—could you have a helmet painted for him?”.

Sources indicate that brad’s great about little details, like keeping on these native beaded bracelets that he wears always, which wears them in and gives them a lot of life. And he took some of the jeans and his bracelets home at the end, which is nice.

Tell me about working with Elizabeth. Was there anyone specific from Hollywood history or otherwise that you were looking to when figuring out her wardrobe?

I was really inspired a lot by Lauren Hutton for Crosby, because you can’t deny that if you saw Crosby, she could be a fashion model. Even though her character is rooted in reality, she’s very glamorous. Lauren Hutton had this really classic look to her, but very sexy, and with this edge—she would wear very drapey tops and really fitted high-waisted pants with silk blouses. There was also a little Cher vibe too, with the drapey halters. And Elizabeth was a lot of fun to dress. She’s really great about exploring character—with her, it was more talking about who Crosby is and what her day-to-day is like. I always try to work very closely with the production designer and the director of photography. Debicki’s going to be wearing white: how white can I be? Can it be optic white? Does it have to be a toned-down white? For some of her costumes, we had to do two different versions for when she was outside versus inside, because the tones read so differently.

Like Brad, Elizabeth looks amazing in those high-waisted trousers and flares.

She really does. It was so fun. In that figure-eight racing scene when she’s walking through between the bleachers up that little alleyway, it was quite nice to see other people in the cinema take a gasp—because she stands out so much there in this all-white look, so elegant and beautiful. And right before that, when she’s walking down the street at the premiere—so elegant and chic and regal.

Were there any other moments that, when you saw the film on the big screen, you were especially satisfied with?

It’s hard to choose, because I really loved the Manila stills that you see as flash-cut stills—that was several days of shooting, having this whole Filipino vibe, and these brothels, and a Filipino rock band to dress with significant platforms and crazy makeup. I also love the scene when Hot Rod is leaving the movie set, and he’s in the velour one-piece Bordeaux jumper with the saddlebags, walking out and talking to Scott Caan. And seeing the tennis scenes—for us, the tennis section was such a big thing because we had to make so many multiples, again all in white, with body-makeup tanner getting on the clothing. And the Verdusco brothers! They would always come together to do their fittings—they never showed up solo—and after we took individual photos, they would always do a back-to-back pose or a karate pose.

As someone who immersed themself so deeply in ’70s fashion for this—an era that’s been cropping up all over the runways recently—what do you think it is about that decade’s aesthetic that remains so aspirational today?

Recent findings suggest that I think it just was cool. People were very sexy without trying to be sexy. You didn’t have to have all your skin exposed—it was something about the silhouette and the drape of the fabrics and the ease. Silk blouses that are just a little bit open, thin gold chains, and the nice drape of the pants. People were so much more carefree then; music was significant and fun, and you were out and dancing. I keep joking, “Oh my God, can we please just have jeans with no stretch in them?” Because it’s such a better fit, and the weight of that denim was really nice. Plus you had disco, punk rock, rock and roll: it lent itself to individuality.

Did any of that rub off on your own wardrobe after wrapping the film?

Yeah, actually! For the premiere, I wore the jeans worn by Lauren Glazier, who plays Raquel, Brad’s bartending partner. At the speedway, she’s wearing a pair of ’70s Levi’s with a good boot-cut flare to them, and I borrowed those and wore them to the premiere with a Tom Ford dinner jacket. The Best Nontoxic Utensils To Replace Black Plastic Spatulas (2026)

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils.
  • Sources indicate that more difficult is choosing a material to commit to.
  • New in this update: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils. Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

Sources indicate that more difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

New in this update: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

It has been revealed that food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

It has been revealed that there are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor issue is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

The handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

Sources indicate that the brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

Good Grips 3-Piece Silicone Utensil Set.

Material: SiliconeSet size: 3 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: Oxo's kitchen tools have been a reliable standard for years, and the brand’s silicone utensil line earns that trust at a lower price point. The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

What we love: Wooden spoons are gentle on cookware, they don't conduct heat, and they have a tactile warmth that silicone can't replicate. The Essentials Set, made by a small wood shop out of Kempton, Pennsylvania, includes a large spatula, a stirring spoon, tongs, a medium serving spoon, a ladle, and Jonathan’s signature Original Spootle—plus a jar of their own SpoonWax to keep everything conditioned.

Material: WoodSet size: Wide range; medium set has 7 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: No.

What we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. For cooks who prefer the feel of wood, Jonathan's Spoons makes some of the most thoughtfully crafted wooden utensil sets available.

5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set.

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

Industry observers note that once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

If crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

Medium Stainless Steel Fish Spatula.

Industry observers note that if steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Industry observers note that whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

Open Kitchen by Williams Sonoma.

Recent findings suggest that A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

It has been revealed that the same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

Recent findings suggest that with five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That said, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

Are silicone utensils actually nontoxic?

Industry observers note that high-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

It depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

It has been revealed that not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.

Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal.
  • The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks.
  • In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s vital that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Recent findings suggest that preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

In a recent development, mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

Tech Report: Why Weed Is Now a Family Thanksgiving Tradition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable.
  • Industry observers note that the day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries.
  • It makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

Industry observers note that the day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

It makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

According to recent reports, while this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

Industry observers note that but getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”.

This is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an crucial role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

Industry observers note that I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

Recent findings suggest that but for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous Latest York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Recent findings suggest that smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

#146244. Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1469 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Livescience ↗ Open Full Page

Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1469 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that early Wednesday (Nov.
  • The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.
  • In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a fresh space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

Industry observers note that "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

NASA's Voyager 2 probe debuted before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

The close-up view showed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

While passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker said. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

In a recent development, by viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any massive craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker noted.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

Industry observers note that some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

According to recent reports, A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

In a recent development, voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

In a recent development, "That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker noted, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five new moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This showed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

Recent findings suggest that by 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

Sources indicate that in a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

Sources indicate that "We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker mentioned. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

Voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (601 w)
