Industry News: I Learned How Baby Carrots Are Made & Haven't Bought Them Since—Here's Why

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that as a lover of all veggies, I love every type of carrot out there—except packaged baby carrots.
  • Here’s the truth about baby carrots—and why you might want to think twice about snagging a bag.
  • The bag might claim otherwise, but packaged “baby carrots” are typically larger carrots chopped into 2-inch pieces, then peeled and polished down to that perfect snackable size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as a lover of all veggies, I love every type of carrot out there—except packaged baby carrots. That’s right: those bright orange cylinders with suspiciously perfect rounded corners that lurk in vending machines, school lunchboxes, and convenience store cold cases across our nation. They might be easy to eat on the go and better for you than a bag of Cheetos, but there’s a lot more going on behind the scenes of this seemingly simple healthy snack.

Here’s the truth about baby carrots—and why you might want to think twice about snagging a bag.

The bag might claim otherwise, but packaged “baby carrots” are typically larger carrots chopped into 2-inch pieces, then peeled and polished down to that perfect snackable size. Real baby carrots are immature carrots harvested before they reach full size. They’re sold in bunches—unpeeled, often with the tops still attached.

While a whole carrot has a delicate, nuanced sweetness, the taste of these so-called baby carrots is best described as... factory-fresh. Don’t believe me? Grab a bag of regular carrots and do a side-by-side taste test.

Industry observers note that baby carrots were originally “invented” in the 1980s to make misshapen or broken carrots sellable. This was a smart way to reduce food waste and save money, but it also helped reinforce the unrealistic expectation that produce must look perfect in order to taste good. Today, baby-cut carrots are grown and processed to meet specific standards for size and shape, all to produce those identical little orange cylinders.

Here’s the bottom line: When you buy a bag of baby carrots, you’re buying into a world that’s seemingly as obsessed with unnatural perfection as the modern-day beauty industry.

Energy conservation is top of mind for consumers these days, but making baby carrots look so uniform takes a lot of machinery. After they’re sorted, they chop the carrots into roughly 2-inch pieces and shave them—twice. Then, they go through a rough cutter, which gives them a general shape, before being polished to create those unrealistically perfect rounded edges. That’s a lot of extra work to make something that was completely edible to begin with look a certain way.

It has been revealed that to prevent bacterial growth, baby carrots may be rinsed with a diluted chlorine solution before packaging. They’re then rinsed with water, and the chlorine treatment itself is an “acceptable” food-safety practice which doesn’t make baby carrots unsafe to eat. Still, do you really want your “fresh” snack to have undergone chlorine treatments of any kind? For me, that’s a hard no, and I’d rather buy whole carrots and wash and cut them myself.

Sources indicate that because baby carrots have been peeled and cut, they're more prone to drying out and developing something called “carrot blush,” a thin white film caused by dehydration. The film itself is harmless, but it certainly doesn’t make them look appetizing. Worse, they can turn slimy inside the bag, even before you open it. And that’s downright gross.

Industry observers note that prices vary depending on where you shop, but baby-cut carrots can cost more per pound than regular whole carrots. You're essentially paying extra for someone else to handle the peeling, cutting, and polishing. For a task that takes barely any time at home, I'd rather keep the difference in my wallet.

Seriously. Enjoy the taste and texture of whole carrots, potentially save some money, and skip the extra processing by simply buying a bag of whole carrots and cutting them yourself. It’ll take you less time than you spent reading this article.

Breaking: Sheet-Pan Chicken Caesar Salad

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp.
  • Lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

It has been revealed that whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

Lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

Sources indicate that transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Recent findings suggest that add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

Latest Update: The Scoop with Kolor’s Taro Horiuchi: On His Zara Collab

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week.
  • Sources indicate that this week’s guest is Taro Horiuchi, who took over the creative direction of Japanese brand Kolor from its founder Junichi Abe, a couple of years ago.
  • Before all that, Taro studied photography at London’s Kingston University and fashion design at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, alongside Demna and Glenn Martens, who were in the year above and below, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week. This will be a way for the Vogue Business community to synthesize and reflect on the latest headlines and get a little inside scoop every Friday.

Sources indicate that this week’s guest is Taro Horiuchi, who took over the creative direction of Japanese brand Kolor from its founder Junichi Abe, a couple of years ago. Before that, Taro was running his namesake womenswear label, which he released after moving to France in 2010, as well as a menswear line called TH Product, founded in 2018 (the two merged when he took over Kolor in 2025).

Before all that, Taro studied photography at London’s Kingston University and fashion design at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, alongside Demna and Glenn Martens, who were in the year above and below, respectively. The thread that seems to bind Taro’s work together is turning basic garments on their heads, which is also what he sought to do in his most recent collaboration with a little conglomerate called Zara. I called him up to discuss that and more.

It has been revealed that on December 3, we will be launching a collaboration with Zara. We are hosting a pop-up in Tokyo on December 2, and the global launch will be the following day. It’s the first global collaboration we’ve announced since I took over as creative director in 2025, so I feel honored to be in this position. The collection will span womenswear, menswear, and childrenswear. It’s the first time Kolor is making kids’ clothing, so that was an interesting challenge for us.

Shots from the Kolor x Zara campaign. It’s the brand’s first global collaboration since Horiuchi took over as creative director from founder Junichi Abe in 2025.

What was it like designing children’s clothes then?

The core challenge for us in this project was expressing the brand without the high pricing and intricate details. We wanted to make good, interesting clothes regardless of whether it was for children or adults. However, there are constraints when it comes to making clothes for children, both in terms of the textiles you can use and because the accessories and the parts on the clothing are very small. That was definitely a learning experience for us, which we took on happily.

According to recent reports, can you tell me a little bit about the collection? What was the inspiration behind it?

So the theme for this project is “World Uniform”. It’s something we do at Kolor: take something basic and turn it into something a little different. Fans of Kolor are always on the cutting edge of fashion, and they are always seeking something upcoming. But those who shop at Zara are looking for clothes for their daily lives. So our challenge was to find the perfect balance between familiar and inspirational.

Behind the scenes of the Kolor x Zara campaign shoot. The collection’s theme, “World Uniform”, reflects Kolor’s habit of taking basic garments and making them “a little different”.

For sure, there are those who go to Zara for basics, but I’d argue that’s changing because of all the luxury brand collaborations Zara orchestrates, including the one with Kolor.

Recent findings suggest that one thing that really stood out to me through this experience was the very high quality of fabrics and operations that Zara offers. My family and friends wear a lot of Zara, though I personally haven’t, so I wasn’t aware of the way they work. But the whole process was very inspirational to me. Both the product quality and the speed of responding were quite remarkable.

Sources indicate that I remember when Zara released in Greece; I was about 8 or 9. My mother was delighted because she could buy cheap but nice clothes for us. I still have some of those sweaters from 30 years ago, and my son wears them now. Has it been fun to work with Zara’s manufacturing resources?

It has been revealed that for sure. When it comes to any collaboration, it doesn’t make sense for me to make anything you can make alone. I am very happy to say we managed to realize something that Kolor couldn’t have made on its own, and I believe Zara feels the same way about us.

A look from Kolor x Zara, which launches globally on December 3 after a pop-up in Tokyo on December 2.

You’ve taken over Kolor from its founder. It feels like a tough gig to follow a founder who is still involved and alive. But if we look at people like Julian Klausner at Dries Van Noten and Haider Ackermann at Tom Ford, maybe that’s part of the success recipe? How do you work with Junichi Abe, and is there a lot of pressure to match him?

In a recent development, I’ll answer your second question about pressure first. Of course, I feel the pressure, and I also respect Abe-san incredibly. Whether it’s a recipe for success, I’m not sure yet. What I can say is that the core value and DNA of a fashion brand aren’t something you can build in one day. It takes time. All I can do is what Abe-san told me to do at the very beginning of my time at Kolor: “Don’t repeat what I could. Just make Kolor unique to you,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that there are quite a few open positions at the significant luxury houses at the moment, and we expect them to be filled any day now. Does the constant change-up in creative directors affect the way you and other designers work or view the industry?

According to recent reports, things change much faster than when I started in fashion around maybe 2005. As I was saying earlier, building a brand takes time because it needs to have a culture and a philosophy. The compatibility of the brand and the designer is very important too in all that. In that sense, speedy changes are not good because they don’t allow the two to get to know each other.

Kolor x Zara. Horiuchi notes the collaboration let him make something Kolor “couldn’t have made on its own”, thanks to Zara’s fabrics and production speed.

Industry observers note that applications for the 2027 LVMH prize are now open. You won the Diesel Award at ITS 20 years ago. How necessary are those awards and prizes to young designers?

I graduated from the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp in 2007, and I am still so thankful to Barbara (Franchin, founder and director of ITS) and Renzo (Rosso, founder of Diesel and founder and chairman of OTB) for the opportunity. Looking back now, this was a substantial turning point in my career. It wasn’t so much about winning the award, but more about the people I met. Demna was in the year above me at Antwerp, and together we organized an exhibition about Japan. At the Diesel award, I met Matthieu Blazy, who is now at Chanel. So, for me, those prizes and competitions are meaningful because of the communities they draw together. If you want to tell what the future of the industry will be in 20 years, you should look at who is entering those competitions now.

But I have a concern about the future of the industry. When I was a student, the tuition fees for Antwerp were around €1,000 per year. Now, for non-EEA students, it’s between €13,000 and €25,000. The people who can’t afford such high tuition will not be entering the fashion industry. Demna wouldn’t have been at Antwerp if the tuition was any more expensive. So maybe, one suggestion for the organizations that support those awards would be to focus more on scholarships and grants.

To see whether any of them are worth the A-list endorsements, we tasted a selection of their most popular red wines. Here are the ones that won over Delish editors.

In a recent development, cameron Diaz's wine brand, Avaline, specializes in bottles made with organically farmed grapes and minimal additives. Avaline's red blend is made in France with Rhône varietals like Grenache and Syrah.

According to recent reports, our editors appreciated its light- to medium-bodied flavor and bone-dry finish. Notes of red fruit and light spice add just enough depth to keep each sip interesting. And at $24 per bottle, this is a solid table wine that tastes much more expensive than it is.

In a recent development, reality TV legend Lisa Vanderpump is no stranger to the food and beverage business. In addition to operating six restaurants, she’s also the mind behind her eponymous wine brand. And LVP’s Sonoma County Cabernet Sauvignon is as elegant and sophisticated as she is.

Sources indicate that while other Cabernets can be bold and intense, this wine's beauty lies in its subtlety. One editor described it as a “summer Cab” because of its soft, delicate fruit profile. The flavor is complex without feeling too rich or heavy, making it an ideal red for dinner. And at $26 a bottle, it’s a good deal, too.

Industry observers note that famed film director Francis Ford Coppola isn’t just known for his Oscar-winning movies—he’s also a prolific winemaker. He sold his namesake winery to Delicato Family Wines in 2021, but the lineup is still just as strong as it was under his leadership.

Industry observers note that we enjoyed all of Coppola’s reds, but the Archimedes Cabernet Sauvignon was a clear standout. Made with California-grown grapes and aged for 20 months in French and American oak barrels, this wine delivers what our editors described as the quintessential Cab, with a full-bodied, smooth flavor and notes of dark fruit and tobacco.

Depending on the vintage and retailer, prices can start around $70 and climb past $100. But if you want to impress both the film buffs and wine snobs in your life, it’s worth the splurge.

Sources indicate that this chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling).

Sources indicate that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

Industry observers note that place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Industry observers note that pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

To serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

This Is Why Your Mashed Potatoes Are Gluey (and How to Fix It)

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Consider this your mashed potato primer, complete with tips on how to fix gluey mashed potatoes and how to prevent them from the start.

My mom’s potato masher is one of my favorite kitchen tools, from its retro design to the thick, grid-patterned bottom that hasn’t bent or warped over the years, despite heavy use. I attributed her consistently perfect fluffy mashed potatoes to this simple tool, even when she was experimenting with new mashed potato ideas. And it turns out there is some truth to it because it created smooth mashed potatoes rapidly yet thoroughly, preventing her from pummeling the spuds into a sticky, gummy mess.

Industry observers note that you see, overworked potatoes are the biggest reason for gluey mashed potatoes, so using the right tool is the best way to prevent them in the first place. And if you came here because your potatoes are already gummy, we have some helpful tips for how to fix gluey mashed potatoes after the fact.

The biggest culprit for gluey mashed potatoes is overworked potatoes. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and a little bit of starch is a good thing. Just as aquafaba (starchy cooked chickpea liquid) can be whipped into a rich vegan mayonnaise, potato starch thickens mashed potatoes and contributes to a creamy texture. But there is a limit.

As you mash chunks of potatoes into a mostly smooth mixture, the spud’s cell walls collapse, freeing the starch within those cells. The more you mash, the more cells are broken down, and the thicker, starchier and gummier the potatoes become. This can happen when you mash potatoes too long by hand, but it happens more rapidly when using electric tools.

It has been revealed that food processors and immersion blenders have incredibly fast, sharp blades. As they whip around, they cut through the potatoes’ cells so rapidly that the once silken mash becomes gluey in a flash. I can’t urge you strongly enough to pass on these tools when mashing potatoes.

There are three components to avoiding gluey mashed potatoes: Choosing the right potato, using the right tool and considering temperature.

Sources indicate that for starters, choose a starchy or all-purpose potato, like a russet or Yukon Gold. These potatoes are relatively low in moisture, helping the potato break down into a creamy mixture. They’ll give you more wiggle room as you mash than waxy potatoes, so the potatoes will turn out delicious even if you lose yourself in exuberant mashing.

Sources indicate that next, use the right kitchen tool for the job and reach for a potato masher, food mill or ricer. These handheld tools give you more control over speed and power as you mash. I prefer a potato masher with a crisscross grid pattern over those with a wavy design because there’s less open space, making each mash more productive.

Finally, warm your butter and milk before adding them to the potatoes. This step may sound finicky, but it prevents the warm potato starches from seizing against cold ingredients and becoming dense. Switch to a spatula and stir them in to keep a gentle touch and retain a fluffy texture.

It has been revealed that you’ll never be able to totally remove the excess starch and get rid of the gluey texture without starting over, but you may be able to improve it. Adding more fat or liquid can improve the mouthfeel, and stirring in other ingredients can alter the overall texture.

Sources indicate that if your potatoes are truly a gluey mess, don’t fret; you can repurpose the potatoes by turning them into leftover mashed potato recipes. Here are some of my favorite ways to use gluey mashed potatoes:.

Sources indicate that knowing what types of potatoes are best for which recipes can save you a lot of grief—and this knowledge will go a long way to preventing gluey potatoes. For the creamiest, smoothest, lightest-as-air mashed potatoes, go with a starchy russet potato. Some people like using all-purpose Yukon Gold potatoes for their naturally buttery flavor, but I prefer to use all russets (or a blend of russets and Yukon Golds for flavor).

It’s best to avoid waxy potatoes, like red or fingerling potatoes, for mashed potato recipes. They keep their shape when they’re cooked, which is why they’re better for potato salads and soups than creamy mashes. They do make an excellent smashed potato, though, if you’re looking to do something a little bit different with your side dish.

As with all cooking rules, this one is made to be broken. If you only have red potatoes in the pantry, you can still use them to make mashed red potatoes. Just keep the potatoes a little bit chunkier so they don’t get gummy. And make sure you refer to them as a “rustic” mash when you bring them to the table to properly temper expectations.

This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.
  • The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.
  • Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the upcoming Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the upcoming Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries stated on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”.

Industry observers note that departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It has been revealed that it’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island remarked in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of fresh well-paying union jobs.”.

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

In a recent development, "We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., mentioned in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the newly introduced Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

Recent findings suggest that “One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., noted in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”.

In a recent development, sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

According to recent reports, absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

According to recent reports, honestly, we can’t think of anything better than a galette. They've got all the delicious elements of pie—flaky, buttery crust and tender baked fruit—but none of the fussy technique. With galettes, you don’t have to worry about any crimping, latticework, or blind baking. Sometimes, it's okay to take the easy road. This classic apple galette is one of our favorite examples. Warm, comforting, and bursting with sweet, spiced flavor, it’s everything you love about apple pie with a fraction of the effort.

What People Are Saying:“I've already made this twice. Really really nice recipe. So fast and simple, not too sweet and not at all goopy. This will be my go-to filling for apple galettes from now on.” - PurpleRing.

Industry observers note that first, combine the apples, brown sugar, lemon juice, cinnamon, and salt in a large bowl. Then, preheat the oven to 400° and prepare a baking sheet by lining it with parchment paper. Coat a clean surface with a dusting of flour, then roll the chilled pie dough into a 12” circle that is about ⅛” thick. Transfer the dough to the baking sheet.

In a recent development, arrange the apple slices on top of the dough in alternating rows, leaving about a 1 ½” border around the edge. Then, fold the dough edge nearest to you toward the center and rotate the baking sheet, repeating this step until all 4 edges of the dough are folded in toward the fruit.

Brush the egg wash over the crust and sprinkle demerara sugar over the top. Then place the galette into the oven to bake for 40 to 45 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the fruit is fragrant and tender. Remove the galette from the oven and transfer it to a cooling rack to cool completely before slicing and serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

According to recent reports, A galette is essentially an open-faced pie. Thinly sliced apples are tossed in cinnamon and sugar and layered on top of a single sheet of pie crust. The crust is folded over the apples in a rough circle and baked until the crust is flaky. Apple pie has a top and bottom crust and is usually formed in a pie dish. The extra crust and overall shape are the only real differences, and for the apple obsessed, galettes provide the perfect ratio of crust to filling.

It has been revealed that anything you'd serve with an apple pie would work here as well. That means your favorite ice cream, frozen yogurt, caramel sauce, or candied nuts would be great galette sidekicks.

Any leftover galette can be stored for up to 4 days in the refrigerator.

I've broken down the differences between the lines below, and the defining details about specific models in each line that are on sale right now. And be sure to bookmark this story because we’ll patch it with more Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals on Nespresso coffee makers and espresso machines as they happen.

Introduced in 2014, Nespresso’s Vertuoline modernized the brand’s original pressure brew method and marked the true beginning of Nespresso espresso and coffee machines. Most Vertuo machines feature just one button and brew both coffee and espresso-style shots using a centrifugal method. Once you choose your preferred pod based on style, roast, and cup size, the machine takes care of the rest. That’s because the rim of every dome-shaped Vertuo capsule features a barcode that tells the Nespresso Vertuo machine how much water and what extraction speed to use for each pod—and can brew everything from a single and double espresso shot to a 14-ounce cup of coffee. Some Vertuo machines can even fill an 18-ounce carafe from a single coffee pod.

The very first Vertuo machine released more than a decade ago is still kicking, and it's one of the best values you can get.

Sources indicate that enabled with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connectivity, the Nespresso Vertuo Next can brew 18 ounces of coffee from a single pod. If you’re intrigued by the tech or pod yield, it’s worth a try—especially considering Nespresso’s 30-day return policy, warranty, and reputation for maintenance and machine repairs.

Vertuo Next Coffee with Aeroccino Milk Frother.

Nespresso Vertuo Pop + Aeroccino Milk Frother.

The newest Vertuo machine, the Vertuo Lattissima is a one-touch machine that makes coffee, espresso, cappuccinos, and latte macchiatos at the push of a button.

Until the Vertuoline was introduced in 2014, the OriginalLine machines were simply known as Nespresso machines. These models brew either single or lungo (Italian for "long") espresso-style shots from any compatible pod using a pressure-driven method. The Original Line features a collection of compact pod-only machines (Nespresso CitiZ, Nespresso Essenza Mini, and Nespresso Pixie) as well as a variety of pricier Creatista and Lattissima models, with built-in steam wands or other automatic milk frothers. Brigadeiro (Brazilian Chocolate Truffles)

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that brigadeiros are like a cross between fudge and Tootsie Rolls in truffle form.
  • Industry observers note that as a major chocolate lover, I’ll eat truffles in almost any form.
  • It has been revealed that brigadeiros start with a can of sweetened condensed milk, plus cocoa powder and butter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that brigadeiros are like a cross between fudge and Tootsie Rolls in truffle form. They're easy to make at home, and even easier to pop in your mouth.

Industry observers note that as a major chocolate lover, I’ll eat truffles in almost any form. Brigadeiros have the familiar flavor and fudgy center of a really good chocolate truffle, but they’re even easier to make because they don’t require melting any chocolate. Everything happens in one small saucepan, and the only difficult part is waiting for the mixture to chill.

It has been revealed that brigadeiros start with a can of sweetened condensed milk, plus cocoa powder and butter. The butter is key to carrying the flavor of the cocoa powder and giving the bite-sized treats their signature soft bite. They end up as glossy little chocolate balls covered in sprinkles that taste halfway between a chocolate truffle and a piece of fudge: dense and chewy with a deep cocoa flavor and a center so creamy it nearly melts on contact.

Sources indicate that brigadeiros are Brazilian confections made by cooking a mixture of sweetened condensed milk, cocoa and butter until it’s thick. Once cooled, the mixture is rolled into bite-size balls. A Brazilian birthday party isn’t complete without a tray of brigadeiros, but they also show up at weddings, baby showers and holiday gatherings. Some cooks skip the rolling altogether and eat the soft mixture with a spoon, a style called brigadeiro de colher.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

In a small saucepan, combine the sweetened condensed milk, cocoa powder and butter. Cook, stirring constantly, on medium-low heat until the mixture is thickened, 8 to 10 minutes. Transfer the mixture to a medium bowl. Refrigerate it, covered, for two hours or until it’s firm enough to be rolled.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Shape the chilled mixture into 1-inch balls. Roll the balls in chocolate sprinkles.

Editor’s Tip: Rub a little butter on your palms before rolling, and grease them again every few balls. This will keep the mixture from sticking and give each truffle a smooth surface.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

It has been revealed that keep brigadeiros in an airtight container in the refrigerator. Store them in paper candy cups or in a single layer separated by parchment so they don’t stick together. Cold brigadeiros get firm, so let them sit out for about 15 minutes before serving to bring back their soft, fudgy centers.

Brigadeiros last up to one week in an airtight container in the refrigerator. They taste best within the first few days while the sprinkles are still crisp.

Sources indicate that yes, you can make brigadeiros ahead of time. Cook the chocolate mixture up to two days in advance and keep it covered in the refrigerator, then roll and coat the truffles the day you strategy to serve them. If the mixture is too stiff to scoop, let it stand at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes.

It has been revealed that yes, brigadeiros freeze well. Arrange the rolled truffles on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze them until they’re firm, about one hour, then transfer them to an airtight container and freeze them for up to three months. Thaw them overnight in the refrigerator.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

When the brigadeiro mixture stays soft and sticky even after chilling, it almost always means that it needs more time on the stove. Scrape it back into the saucepan and cook it over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for a few more minutes until it thickens and pulls away from the bottom of the pan in one mass. Watch the mixture closely because overcooking will turn it stiff and grainy.

It has been revealed that no, brigadeiros won’t work with regular milk. Brigadeiros depend on the concentrated sugar and milk solids in sweetened condensed milk to cook down into a thick fudge that can be rolled. If you’re out of it, you can make your own sweetened condensed milk by simmering whole milk and sugar until the mixture reduces by about half.

Million-Dollar Mac & Cheese

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in my opinion, mac & cheese is a must-have on any holiday table. If you’re looking to take the classic from good to million-dollar-price-tag-worthy, then this is the recipe for you. My million-dollar mac & cheese is what happens when you decide to take basic mac & cheese on a shopping spree to the fanciest cheese shop you know and shower it with gold leaf. Showcasing a trifecta of bougie (and delicious) cheeses and a crispy, crunchy panko topping, this irresistible comfort food will take center stage on any table it hits.

The cheeses:Most of the great mac & cheeses I’ve ever eaten contain three distinct cheeses: a base melting cheese, a tangy cheese with some character, and a sharper accent cheese. For this million-dollar mac, I chose Pecorino Romano as my accent, but went slightly rogue with the other two and paired fontina and French raclette, which both melt well and have quite a bit of funk. French raclette is particularly great for a mac & cheese sauce since it becomes almost fondue-like when melted, giving you cheese pulls beyond your wildest dreams.

The combination of these three cheeses is worth that million-dollar label, so even if you don’t typically buy these cheeses, I urge you to seek them out for this mac. That said, if you absolutely can’t find them, you could try combining comté and Camembert or Gruyère and brie with the Pecorino to give you a similar result.

The crispy topping:With a dish as rich and creamy as this mac & cheese, a crispy, crunchy topping is key. Pre-toasting the panko in butter on the stove ensures a truly golden-brown, delicious topping, without the nail-biting broiler-watching session. Using a higher butter-fat European-style butter here (as well as in the sauce) brings additional richness, ensuring this million-dollar mac is as decadent as it should be. In testing, I found that the breadcrumbs on top of the mac didn’t brown much more when they were on top of the mac in the oven, but if you’re concerned about them getting too dark, you can always lightly tent the pan with foil.

The gold leaf topping is a fun way to cue the whole “million-dollar” thing, but it’s totally not necessary. Use it if you want, but don’t feel obligated!

Storage:Any leftover mac & cheese can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave, covered, in 30-second bursts until warmed through or, if you have enough, in the oven in a covered ceramic dish.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A 1991 tuna salad snack started it all, and yes, there's a fan club.

It’s the morning after Thanksgiving. The good dishes are still drying, the fridge is a Tetris board of foil-wrapped leftovers and you’re standing over the kitchen sink eating cold stuffing with your bare hands. No plate, no judgment.

According to recent reports, as it turns out, there’s an entire holiday dedicated to this very specific dining experience. It’s called Sinkie Day, and it’s been around since long before TikTok made girl dinner a thing.

For that, we have Norm Hankoff to thank. An advertising consultant from California, he had his lightbulb moment in 1991 “while wolfing down some tuna salad over his sink, using extra-strength potato chips as utensils,” according to a 1997 Associated Press report.

According to recent reports, convinced he couldn’t be the only one, Hankoff founded the International Association of People Who Dine Over the Kitchen Sink and declared the day after Thanksgiving Sinkie Day. By 1997, more than 1,000 people had joined, and each one received a membership certificate stamped with a double sink and the group’s motto: “Everybody does it. Sinkies proudly admit it.”.

Naturally, there was a cookbook—or rather, a don’t-cook book. Published by a firm cheekily called Digester’s Reader, The Official Sinkies Don’t Cook Book included such culinary masterpieces as “cakeless frosting” and “meat loaf in your fist.” Other recipes called for little more than a handful of mashed potatoes or a piece of chocolate cake dunked in a glass of milk.

Industry observers note that hankoff even set his sights on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. When Hillary Clinton was looking for a chef in 1994, he sent her a copy of his book and suggested the first family give sink-side snacking a try. No word on whether they took his advice, but the White House did send him a thank-you letter.

The beauty of Sinkie Day, which falls on Friday, Nov. 27, this year, is that it’s perhaps the only food holiday that actively encourages you to do less. A fridge full of Thanksgiving extras is all it takes, though a few upgrades never hurt:.

Of course, a holiday devoted to leftovers is also a good excuse to brush up on food safety. As long as everything hit the fridge within two hours of cooking, you’ve got three to four days to work your way through it.

It has been revealed that want to treat yourself to five-star brunch without making a ton of dishes—or taking off your pj’s? Hack the classic croque madame by making it in the air fryer. Here, crispy toast is topped with an egg and smothered with ham, cheese, and béchamel for a simpler version of the classic French dish that will transform the comfort of your sofa into a fancy brunch spot in five seconds flat.

How is this a croque madame?A classic croque madame is a toasted ham and cheese sandwich that’s topped with a layer of béchamel, broiled until bubbly, and then topped with a fried egg. This air fryer version takes all those components—toasty bread, fried egg, béchamel, ham, and cheese—and reconfigures them into a form that cooks much easier in the air fryer. You might say it almost looks like a classic egg-in-the-hole, but don’t worry! If you close your eyes, you’ll still taste croque madame.

The microwave béchamel:There’s nothing wrong with making béchamel in a pot on the stove, but making it in the microwave means fewer heavy dishes to clean—and it’s also a great hack to know if you’re somewhere with limited (or no!) stove space. Rather than standing over a pot, whisking constantly, you’ll simply whisk the flour into the melted butter, microwave until it’s bubbling, then whisk in the milk and microwave again. Once it’s thickened, you can fold in the cheese. Though I don’t recommend microwaving after the cheese goes in—that’s a sure way to break your sauce—if it absolutely needs it, you can microwave it for very short bursts just till it melts together.

Delish Official:Eggland's Best Eggs are the Official Eggs of Delish. That means they're the only eggs we're using in our recipe content.

It has been revealed that make-ahead & storage:Once cooked, the air fryer croque madame should be eaten immediately. That stated, the béchamel can be made 2 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator. I recommend gently reheating it before using. I typically do this in the microwave in 15-second increments, stirring in between—this prevents the sauce from breaking.

We’ve Been Using Our Gravy Boats Wrong for Decades—Here’s How You’re Supposed to Use Them

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.
  • I have a particular weakness for antique dishes.
  • Industry observers note that then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.

I have a particular weakness for antique dishes. Most weekends I can be found happily perusing the shelves at thrift and antique stores, where an occasional beautiful piece makes up for an awful lot of cracked mugs and mismatched dinnerware. The gravy boat I use every Thanksgiving was one of those finds. I love it—even though I’ve never been particularly fond of pouring from it. Gravy has an unfortunate tendency to run down the spout rather than into the intended destination—a minor inconvenience of an otherwise lovely piece.

Industry observers note that then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life. Moore, a British antiques expert, explains that what most of us recognize as a pouring spout on a gravy boat may actually have been intended as a place to rest a small ladle. Excuse me? I’d spent years admiring and collecting old dishware, and somehow this particular bit of history had escaped me. More importantly, I was beginning to suspect that my antique boat had been unfairly blamed for an awful lot of spilled gravy.

Ellie Martin Cliffe For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that according to Moore, traditional gravy boats were often intended to be used with small ladles, their handles resting nearly in the notch we’ve come to think of as a spout. In the sort of formal household familiar to anyone who’s watched The Gilded Age, a footman would have served the gravy or sauce by the spoonful rather than by tipping the entire boat over someone’s plate. It’s a rather elegant arrangement, and one that makes considerably more sense to me than trying to coax gravy out of a vessel that seems determined to spill all over the tablecloth.

Industry observers note that moore also offers an explanation for how we got into the habit of pouring. He indicates that around the middle of the 20th century, ceramic manufacturers began doing away with matching ladles to save money. Without the ladles, people started using the boats as little pitchers, and eventually the pouring method became familiar practice.

Of course, some gravy boats really were designed for pouring, and the presence of a spout doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve misunderstood the entire object. Both methods have a history, although I find Moore’s explanation fascinating. A piece of dishware I’ve used for years suddenly makes much more sense, and I rather like the possibility that I might accidentally stumble upon its matching ladle one day while I’m out treasure hunting.

In a recent development, for gravy boats intended to be used with a ladle, the boat stays on the table while guests serve themselves by the spoonful. A small sauce or gravy ladle works perfectly well, even if it wasn’t made to match the boat, and its handle can rest against the spout if the shape allows.

Recent findings suggest that this is especially useful for gravy boats with attached saucers, which can be awkward to tip without sending accumulated drips onto the table. As Etiquetteer notes, ladling sauce is traditional, but pouring is perfectly acceptable when there’s no ladle.

In a recent development, and if your gravy boat pours beautifully, by all means carry on. Mine has never been especially cooperative, and after all these years, I’m rather pleased to discover that there may be a good explanation as to why.

Why ‘Blackout Wednesday’ Has Become One Of The Biggest Drinking Nights Of The Year

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Wednesday isn’t typically a massive night for restaurants and bars—but the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is different.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Wednesday isn’t typically a massive night for restaurants and bars—but the Wednesday before Thanksgiving is different. Most people have the next day off, and college students or young professionals are typically back in their hometowns for the holiday. What better way to kick off the long weekend than to get off your parents’ couch and hit up the local watering hole?

Recent findings suggest that that’s how Thanksgiving Eve came to be known as “Blackout Wednesday” or “Drinksgiving,” one of the busiest drinking nights of the year. A 2023 study found that in 2022, liquor sales grew by 156% and beer sales increased by 85% on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Cocktail orders surged by 69%.

It has been revealed that doorDash has even named the day one of the busiest for alcohol deliveries. Among 10 more traditional holidays like Newly introduced Year’s Eve and July 4th, Blackout Wednesday ranks right in the middle. “As families and friends return home for the winter holidays, the day before Thanksgiving has become the fifth most popular day for alcohol delivery,” DoorDash’s website reads.

Going out in your hometown is prime time for idly snooping on people from high school, witnessing some truly unlikely pairings (Tyler and Kayla?!). It’s social and nostalgic, but it’s also a day when one drink can easily turn into one too many.

It’s not all fun and drinking games, however. This unofficial holiday marks the start of so-called “DUI Season,” with checkpoints ramping up before Turkey Day. Your risk of coming into contact with a drunk driver also becomes 55% higher than on average days.

Short-term risks of heavy drinking and blacking out include vomiting, seizures, depression, and accidental injuries, as well as next-day anxiety and depression. Long-term, recurring binges are linked to liver damage, high blood pressure, and mental health issues. Alcohol-induced blackouts can also occur more rapidly after just a few drinks, especially if you are taking certain medications, drink on an empty stomach, or have a low body weight.

It’s totally valid to blow off some steam (or get out of chopping celery), just initiative it smart. With actually-delicious mocktails, non-alcoholic beers, and ride-shares, there’s very little reason to put yourself—or others—in danger, especially during the holidays.

Hosts and guests alike can benefit from making a plan for keeping everyone safe until well after New Year’s Day by providing plenty of non-alcoholic options at gatherings, opting in on a “Dampsgiving,” checking in with loved ones (and designated drivers) before they hit the road, and always making sure there’s a spot on the couch for anyone who helped themselves to a few too many eggnog espresso martinis.

Tech Report: Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

📅 28 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon.
  • Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp.
  • Recent findings suggest that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 glitch of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Recent findings suggest that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Recent findings suggest that absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

According to recent reports, IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

According to recent reports, IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

This beloved American fast-food chain is known for its ButterBurgers and frozen custard. Can you guess?

Sources indicate that pop the cheese curds, Wisconsin! Forbes just released its first-ever America’s Favorite Restaurants list, and the No. 1 spot didn’t go to Chick-fil-A, McDonald’s or any coastal cult favorite (lookin’ at you, In-N-Out). It went to Culver’s.

According to recent reports, to build the ranking, Forbes partnered with data and insights manufacturer HundredX to poll more than 100,000 Americans about 100 restaurants, from sit-down chains and fast-food spots to coffee shops that serve food. The survey considered eight categories: taste, price, food quality, menu, value, atmosphere, cleanliness and speed.

Industry observers note that the Midwestern chain known for its ButterBurgers, frozen custard, crinkle-cut fries and breaded cheese curds scored extra well in taste and food quality. Honestly, anyone who’s ended a long day with a Concrete Mixer already knew that.

Recent findings suggest that we’ll admit to some hometown pride here. Taste of Home is based in Wisconsin too, so watching a homegrown favorite take it all feels a little like seeing your cousin’s pie win the county fair.

Culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the manufacturer is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

In-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

The biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. But if you’re planning a holiday road trip, it could be worth checking whether there’s a Culver’s along the way. A ButterBurger and a scoop of the Flavor of the Day make a detour worth every mile. And if there’s not one nearby, these Culver’s copycats will do the trick.

Suqaar Digaag (Chicken and Vegetable Sauté)

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Like all suqaar, this chicken suqaar features xawaash and bright peppers, but it skips the potato found in hilib (beef) suqaar.
  • Toast 1 cup (100 g) whole cumin seeds, 1 cup (70 g) whole coriander seeds, ¼ cup (35 g) black peppercorns, 1 small-to-medium piece of cinnamon bark, 2 Tbsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s no exaggeration to say that xawaash is at the heart of Somali cuisine. It is Somali history on a plate—a culinary reminder of Somalia’s centuries of global trade, particularly along the Indian Ocean. Xawaash is what makes many Somali dishes taste distinctly Somali. While every household’s xawaash recipe is its own, typically seven core spices—cumin, coriander, black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and turmeric—are toasted until their fragrance blooms, then blended into an earthy golden-brown powder. Xawaash stores very well and for a long time in an airtight container, though it’s at its peak shortly after it’s made. If you use it often, you can double or triple the recipe for a significant batch.

Like all suqaar, this chicken suqaar features xawaash and bright peppers, but it skips the potato found in hilib (beef) suqaar. It has a hint of heat thanks to the black pepper and optional jalapeño. Suqaar is cooked covered to keep the meat juicy and moist. Serve with the flatbread of your choice (canjeero, muufo, or sabaayad) for a light lunch or over plenty of rice for a more filling dinner.

More tasty chicken thigh recipes here.

Toast 1 cup (100 g) whole cumin seeds, 1 cup (70 g) whole coriander seeds, ¼ cup (35 g) black peppercorns, 1 small-to-medium piece of cinnamon bark, 2 Tbsp. green cardamom pods, and 1½ tsp. whole cloves in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring constantly so the spices don’t burn. The spices are toasted when they have a slightly darker color and become fragrant, 1–2 minutes. Transfer the toasted spices to a blender or spice grinder and blend until they become a fine powder. Transfer to a bowl and mix in ¼ cup (30 g) ground turmeric until it’s fully incorporated and the spice mix is golden brown. Allow to cool completely, then store in an airtight container.

In a medium bowl, combine the juice of ½ lemon, 1 tsp. xawaash, 1 tsp. fine sea salt, ½ tsp. paprika, and ⅛ tsp. ground black pepper. Add 1 lb. (450 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into bite-sized pieces, and mix everything together to coat the chicken. Set aside.

In a large skillet over medium-high heat, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil until loose. Add 1 large yellow onion, halved and sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 minutes, or until the onion is softened. Add 6 garlic cloves, minced, and 1 medium jalapeño, halved, and stir for another minute, then add the chicken in a single layer. Allow it to cook undisturbed for 5 minutes, then turn the pieces over and cook for 3 minutes more, until fully cooked through.

According to recent reports, add the remaining 1½ tsp. xawaash, ¾ cup (12 g) coarsely chopped cilantro leaves, 1 medium red bell pepper, sliced, and 1 medium yellow bell pepper, sliced, and stir to combine. Cover the skillet and turn the heat down to medium-low; cook until the peppers have softened, 10 to 15 minutes. Serve hot.

#146206. White Meat vs. Dark Meat: Which Part Of The Turkey Is Actually Healthier?

White Meat vs. Dark Meat: Which Part Of The Turkey Is Actually Healthier?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that every Thanksgiving, the table splits into two camps.
  • Recent findings suggest that somewhere along the way, dark meat picked up a reputation as the "less healthy" choice.
  • According to recent reports, the color comes down to a protein called myoglobin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that every Thanksgiving, the table splits into two camps. There's Team White Meat, politely asking for "just a slice of breast, please." Then there's Team Dark Meat, already eyeing the drumstick like it's the last Pop-Tart in the box. It's basically Team Edward vs. Team Jacob, but with gravy.

Recent findings suggest that somewhere along the way, dark meat picked up a reputation as the "less healthy" choice. As a dietitian, I get asked about this a lot, especially the week of Thanksgiving. The short answer is that dark meat isn't the villain it's made out to be. The long answer is way more interesting, so grab a fork. Cranberry sauce optional.

According to recent reports, the color comes down to a protein called myoglobin. Myoglobin stores oxygen inside muscle cells, and muscles that work steadily over long periods need more of it. On a turkey, that means the legs and thighs, which the bird uses to stand and walk around all day.

Recent findings suggest that domestic turkeys use their breast muscles far less, so they carry less myoglobin and stay pale. Myoglobin contains heme iron, which matters for nutrition. More on that in a minute.

Recent findings suggest that so when you choose dark meat, you're eating hardworking muscle. That changes its nutritional profile in a few notable ways.

In a recent development, both cuts are excellent sources of protein. A 3-ounce serving of roasted, skinless turkey provides roughly 24 to 25 grams of protein, whether it's white or dark meat. White meat edges ahead by a gram or two, but in practical terms, both will do the job.

If protein is a priority, either cut gets you there. No need to stage a dramatic family intervention over the drumsticks.

Skinless dark meat does have more fat than skinless white meat, typically a few extra grams per 3-ounce serving. Some of that is saturated fat.

Context matters, though. The difference amounts to a few grams on a single plate, not a massive gap. Keeping the skin on also adds more fat to either cut. A slice of breast with crispy skin can end up in a similar ballpark to skinless thigh meat.

Industry observers note that saturated fat and heart health remain an active area of research. A Cochrane systematic review found that reducing dietary saturated fat was linked to a modest reduction in cardiovascular events over time. That finding reflects overall eating patterns across months and years, though, not what you eat at one holiday meal. A few extra grams of fat from turkey thighs won't make or break anyone's health.

Fat also brings flavor and moisture, which is why dark meat rarely turns into the dry, sawdust situation that can happen to an overcooked breast.

According to recent reports, remember myoglobin? Thanks in part to its heme iron, dark meat generally contains more iron than white meat. Heme iron, the type found in animal foods, is generally absorbed more efficiently than the non-heme iron found in plants.

In a recent development, that's meaningful, because iron deficiency is the most common cause of anemia worldwide. It's especially common among people who menstruate, pregnant people, and young children. Turkey thighs won't fix a deficiency on their own, but they can absolutely contribute to your overall iron intake.

According to recent reports, dark meat also delivers noticeably more zinc than white meat. Zinc plays a key role in immune function, wound healing, and taste perception. Not bad for the part of the bird some people skip.

This is where things get fun, because each cut has its own nutritional strengths.

These B vitamins help your body turn food into usable energy. Vitamin B12 also supports nerve function and red blood cell production, and B12 deficiency is more common in older adults and people who eat few animal foods.

It has been revealed that neither cut offers a complete B vitamin package on its own. Together, though? They make a pretty great team.

Industry observers note that not really. It's just different. White meat offers slightly more protein and less fat, plus more niacin and B6. Dark meat has more iron, zinc, and riboflavin, plus richer flavor and a juicier texture. Both provide vitamin B12.

In a recent development, neither one deserves a "good" or "bad" label. Health is shaped by your eating patterns over time, not by which slice you pick from the platter on one Thursday in November.

Recent findings suggest that if you have a specific health condition, a registered dietitian can help you figure out what works best for you. For most people, though, the best turkey is the one you actually enjoy eating.

Industry observers note that pick the cut you love. Better yet, take a little of both. Dark meat isn't a nutritional compromise, and white meat isn't a punishment. They're two parts of the same bird, each with its own strengths.

So go ahead and claim that drumstick. Or the breast. Or both. Your plate, your call. Just save some gravy for the rest of us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A little ingenuity with an ordinary piece of silverware makes for a beautiful holiday cheese board.

As much as I love a big, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen. A good cheese board is almost always part of the festivities in my house. My affection for charcuterie boards is, admittedly, not doing much to challenge the millennial stereotype.

Recent findings suggest that I love choosing cheeses and spreads that complement one another and bringing out some of my favorite serving pieces for the occasion. It’s one of the more enjoyable bits of prepping holiday party appetizers, in part because so much of the work can be done well before anyone arrives. And while I’m happy to devote a little extra time to the presentation, I’m always equally happy to discover a little shortcut that leaves me more time for the people I’m feeding.

In a recent development, one of my favorite recent discoveries is a clever trick for slicing cheese into neat, even pieces using the tines of an ordinary dinner fork. It’s the sort of kitchen trick that seems almost embarrassingly obvious once you’ve seen it.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

In a recent development, start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

This trick is particularly well suited to cheeses like Gouda, cheddar and Gruyere, which are generally firm enough to slice cleanly but pliable enough to take the impression of a fork. I wouldn’t bother with a ripe Brie or a crumbly blue cheese, both of which lend themselves to a less structured presentation anyway.

It has been revealed that I love this trick for fanning slices of cheese around the edge of a charcuterie board or arranging them in pretty, overlapping rows. And given the number of things competing for my attention when I’m entertaining, I’m delighted to delegate the finer points of cheese geometry to a fork.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” remarked a Republican strategist.

It has been revealed that brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

According to recent reports, republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

It has been revealed that republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of Latest Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.
