Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

It has been revealed that for the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host says dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

Sources indicate that I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

Once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

The short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

Industry observers note that A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:.

I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a big breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

In a recent development, first, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a big deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

This is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really key to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

Industry observers note that and I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really key for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

It’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

Sources indicate that thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

In a recent development, “I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

Industry observers note that stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

If your holiday spread always includes a plate of crispy latkes and a round of dirty martinis, these dirty martini latkes are probably your dream mash-up. This playful party app takes everything you love about the classic Hanukkah potato pancake and gives it a cocktail-inspired twist with buttery green olives, pimento peppers, and a tangy blue cheese and vermouth-spiked sour cream for dipping. The blue cheese isn’t mandatory, but if you love an ice-cold filthy martini with a couple of blue cheese stuffed olives in it, you’ll totally understand my vision. Pair these with other Hanukkah favorites for a festive spread that's equal parts nostalgic and fun.

It has been revealed that the latkes:Traditional latkes start with freshly grated potatoes, but frozen shredded hash browns are the secret shortcut here, cutting prep time without sacrificing crispy edges or fluffy centers. The key is squeezing out as much moisture as possible, then fluffing the shreds with a fork so they stay light instead of turning dense. Castelvetrano olives add a rich, buttery flavor, but Spanish queen or manzanilla olives work just as well. If you can find green olives already stuffed with pimento, go ahead and use them—you can skip the extra chopped pimentos altogether.

Industry observers note that make ahead & storage:The vermouth-blue cheese dipping sauce can be made up to 7 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator, making your day-of party prep that much easier. Leftover latkes can be refrigerated for up to 4 days; just reheat them in a 400° oven or air fryer until hot and crisp again for the best texture.

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Our giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant has a filling of frangipane and melted chocolate chips between two light, buttery sheets of puff pastry.

Industry observers note that this giant croissant is practically the size of a sheet pan. The bigger, the better, as they say, but we’re more into its shareable nature and simple-to-make design. Shatteringly crisp puff pastry (store-bought, of course) replaces hard-to-make croissant dough, with extra square footage for both this treat’s iconic croissant fillings: pain au chocolat and almond croissant. Win-win-win. Save this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant for special occasions or holiday mornings.

Preheat the oven to 425°F. On a lightly floured surface, roll out each sheet of puff pastry to a 12×10-inch rectangle. Place one on a parchment-lined 15x10x1-inch baking pan. Top the puff pastry with a second piece of parchment paper and a second 15x10x1-inch baking pan. This keeps the puff pastry from rising too much so it stays flat.

Bake the puff pastry for 15 minutes. Remove the top pan and parchment. Continue baking the puff pastry until it’s golden brown, five to seven minutes longer. Cool the puff pastry on a wire rack. Repeat the same process with the second slice of puff pastry.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, in a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, almond flour and confectioners’ sugar until they’re light and fluffy, two to three minutes. Add the egg and beat well until it’s incorporated.

Place one baked sheet of puff pastry on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Spread two-thirds of the almond filling over it.

In a recent development, sprinkle the chocolate chips evenly all over. Carefully place the second sheet of baked puff pastry over top, and pipe or spread the remaining third of the almond filling on top.

Sprinkle the top with sliced almonds.

Reduce the oven setting to 350°. Bake the croissant just until the filling is set, 18 to 20 minutes longer. Cool the croissant completely on a wire rack before serving.

Just as you’re ready to serve, dust the top with confectioners’ sugar and, if desired, drizzle it with warm hot fudge.

Store leftover giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant in an airtight container in the fridge. It can be kept for up to three days. Just know that it is best enjoyed the day of, as the frangipane will make the puff pastry soggy.

Sources indicate that yes, you can make certain aspects of a giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant ahead of time, but wait to assemble and bake it until you’re ready to serve. You can bake the puff pastry sheets one day ahead, let them cool to room temperature, wrap them tightly in storage wrap and store them at room temperature. Make the frangipane up to two days beforehand and keep it covered in the fridge.

In a recent development, yes, you can make a gluten-free version of this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant. Simply replace the puff pastry with a gluten-free variety. DuFour, Sweet Loren’s and Schar make fantastic gluten-free puff pastry. All other ingredients are naturally gluten free (but do double-check the hot fudge, if you’re using it); just make sure they weren’t processed in a facility that handles wheat.

Serve your giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant with strong coffee or tea. Pair it with other brunch, like egg casseroles, plates of bacon and sausage and a fruit salad. I wouldn’t set out any other sweets—this croissant is plenty!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Recent findings suggest that I thought I knew exactly how I felt about ranch dressing. Then I made Ina's version.

I have a confession to make. I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing. I realize this puts me at odds with a substantial portion of the American population, but I’ve always preferred a good balsamic vinaigrette or a creamy Caesar. And despite making countless salad dressings over the years, I’ve never once felt compelled to make ranch.

Sources indicate that I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch. I found the whole business unappealing, an opinion that has apparently skipped a generation seeing as both of my children now do exactly the same thing. There’s always a bottle of ranch in our refrigerator that was purchased specifically for pizza night, and it has absolutely nothing to do with me.

Then I came across an Instagram reel of Ina Garten making her buttermilk ranch dressing for a wedge salad. I’ve trusted Ina with everything from roast chicken to panna cotta, and if anyone could persuade me to reconsider my longstanding position on ranch, I figured it would be her. So, after decades of avoiding it, I finally made a batch of ranch dressing.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that ina’s recipe makes about 3 cups of dressing, which initially struck me as an ambitious quantity for someone with my history of distatte. Fortunately, it comes together in just a few minutes, and the ingredients are far more fresh and interesting than anything I’d previously associated with ranch.

Combine the scallions, basil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, olive oil, garlic, salt and pepper in a food processor fitted with a steel blade. Puree them for 15 to 20 seconds, until the mixture is smooth.

It has been revealed that add the mayonnaise, Greek yogurt and buttermilk, then blend the dressing again until everything is thoroughly combined. Transfer the dressing to a covered container and refrigerate it for an hour to let the flavors develop.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Sources indicate that that’s really all there is to it. No complicated technique or careful emulsifying, and very little cleanup. The hour in the refrigerator is important, though, since it gives the garlic, herbs and other seasonings time to mingle with the creamy ingredients.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Of course, I expected Ina’s ranch to be better than the bottled varieties I’ve tried. What I didn’t expect was for it to taste like an entirely different dressing.

Industry observers note that the first thing that struck me was how fresh it was. The basil and scallions give it a wonderful, almost garden-like quality, while the garlic and Dijon add savory sharpness that keeps all that creaminess interesting. There’s plenty of richness from the mayonnaise, but the buttermilk, Greek yogurt and lemon juice provide enough acidity to balance it. It’s tangy, herbaceous and wonderfully flavorful—without the heavy, slightly cloying quality I’ve always associated with ranch.

Sources indicate that and the basil! It’s not an herb I would have thought to put in ranch dressing, but it works beautifully. Its flavor comes through clearly without overwhelming the other ingredients, giving the dressing a character all its own.

In her video, Ina serves the dressing over a wedge salad topped with tomatoes and onion. Having already entrusted her with the dressing, I figured I might as well follow her lead with the salad, too. I made my own wedge with Flavor Bombs tomatoes (my favorites), pepitas and crispy pieces of bacon, then spooned a generous amount of ranch over the whole thing. The cold, crunchy lettuce was the perfect backdrop for the dressing, while the sweet tomatoes, salty bacon and nutty pepitas made the whole thing particularly satisfying. I’ve always loved a good wedge salad, but this was easily one of the best I’ve had.

Sources indicate that by the time I’d finished testing and photographing the recipe, nearly half the dressing was gone, and I was already making plans for the rest. I have to admit, I’m even curious to see how it tastes with pizza, which is not something I ever expected to say about ranch dressing.

The green beans:The green beans, a nod to the iconic casserole, are streamlined for the sheet pan, tossed with mushrooms, Parmesan, and thyme-infused butter, and finished with crispy fried onions for that quintessential touch.

According to recent reports, make-ahead & storage:If the idea of making a whole Thanksgiving dinner on a sheet pan in one day feels daunting, here’s a tip—prep some components ahead of time. Most, if not all, of the ingredient chopping, grating, toasting, etc., can be done 2 to 3 days in advance. Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It has been revealed that no ricotta? Reach for a scoop of protein-rich cottage cheese. It's the secret to these tender, moist and protein-rich meatballs.

My kids have never been huge meat eaters. In fact, my son is more likely to polish off a giant bowl of cherry tomatoes than he is to dig into a burger. Meatballs, though, have always been the exception—and these cottage cheese meatballs have been a long-time favorite. My kids love how tender and juicy they are, and I love that they sneak a little extra protein into their diet.

Sources indicate that many traditional meatball recipes already include ricotta cheese, which binds and adds moisture to the meat mixture. Cottage cheese is a natural swap, adding fat that keeps the meatballs irresistibly moist and tender. Once these protein-packed meatballs are simmered in your favorite jarred pasta sauce and served over pasta, people will never guess that cottage cheese is the secret ingredient.

Editor’s Tip: For the softest, most tender meatballs, handle them gently as you shape them. Avoid overhandling or compacting the meat too much (one of Grandma’s best meatball tips), as it can make the meatballs tough and dense.

Sources indicate that I’ve said it before, I’ll say it again: Every holiday table needs a salad. This one was dreamed up for Hanukkah, my family’s second-favorite special occasion after Thanksgiving. Serve it with roast chicken or salmon and you have an objectively perfect meal. It’s bright, crunchy, and decked out with little “latkes.” Potato croutons have popped up in a few places over the years, like The Salad Lab’s own Hanukkah-inspired salad (great minds!), Daniel Humm’s salmon rösti salad from Made Nice, and Ore-Ida’s cutely named CrouTots. My take is as lazy as it gets: frozen tater tots, smashed. The result is ultra-crisp, like the tiniest potato pancake in the world. A salad spinner is a godsend for washing the lettuce and herbs. Any type of apple works (I like Honeycrisp or Fuji) and the fresh horseradish on top is optional. But if you can find it, get it!

More festive Hanukkah recipes this way.

Preheat oven to 425°. Mix together ½ cup sour cream, 3 Tbsp. drained prepared horseradish, 1 Tbsp. distilled white vinegar, a major pinch of kosher salt, and 1 tsp. water in a small bowl, adding more water a little at a time if needed until dressing it drizzle-able. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

It has been revealed that bake 1 lb. frozen tater tots on a large rimmed baking sheet for half the time of package directions (about 10 minutes).

Sources indicate that meanwhile, place 1 small white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, in a small bowl; pour in cold water to cover and add a few ice cubes. Set onions aside.

Sources indicate that tear pull apart leaves from 1 lb. romaine lettuce (about ⅔ head) and/or Little Gem lettuce (4–5 heads) and tear large leaves in half. Place in a large bowl. Remove tough stems from 1 bunch dill and 1 bunch parsley; discard. Coarsely tear remaining leaves and tender stems. Add to lettuce.

Remove tater tots from oven and, using oven mitts for safety, lay another baking sheet directly on top; firmly press down on tots to flatten. (If you don’t have a second baking sheet, use a heatproof measuring cup or mug instead.) Return tater tots to oven and bake until deep golden brown and crisp, 10–20 minutes.(If your oven has a convection setting, now is a great time to use it.).

Recent findings suggest that drain reserved onion and pat dry. Thinly slice 2 large apples (about 1 lb.). Add both to bowl with lettuce and herbs.

Industry observers note that drizzle 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and add a significant pinch of flaky sea salt. Toss to combine, then mound salad on a platter. Evenly scatter tater tots and ¾ cup pomegranate seeds over.

Serve salad with remaining dressing for drizzling over and peeled fresh horseradish (if using) for grating over.

#146190. Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1157 w)

Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • Recent findings suggest that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • According to recent reports, for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Recent findings suggest that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, Newly introduced York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

According to recent reports, for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

It has been revealed that originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, remarked that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

According to recent reports, wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit New York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she notes. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Industry observers note that spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, indicates that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to fresh takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she says. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Hold the jelly! The iconic peanut butter brand is taking a surprisingly savory direction with its latest product.

Who says peanut butter doesn’t deserve a spot in your dinner rotation?

In a recent development, jif, the beloved peanut butter brand that’s been a staple in American pantries for decades, has ventured into some unexpected territory. If you’re a frequent Costco shopper, you might want to take a closer look the next time you’re browsing the instant noodles.

Some locations of the warehouse retailer are now carrying a six-pack of Jif stir-fry-style instant ramen noodles, giving shoppers an entirely different way to enjoy the taste of peanut butter.

But so far, the reviews among shoppers are mixed.

“Anyone who thinks this sounds gross has never had Thai food and it shows. Peanut butter noodles are kinda awesome,” one fan wrote in a video making the rounds on Instagram.

“Prolly fire w some chili oil,” another claimed.

“I had this last month. Pretty good for instant noodles,” another stated.

A fourth wrote, “As a peanut butter [connoisseur] I don’t approve this.”.

“Diabolical waste of resources,” a fifth claimed.

Peanuts have long been incorporated into savory noodle dishes, particularly in Asian-inspired cooking. Still, seeing the recognizable Jif logo on a package of instant noodles might have you raising your eyebrows. Rather than replicating the sweet, creamy taste of a spoonful of peanut butter, the noodles take a more savory approach. The seasoning contains peanut flour alongside ingredients like soy sauce, garlic and artificial beef flavor.

Jif has another product worth keeping an eye out for at Costco. The brand’s peanut butter and chocolate pretzel Snappers hit shelves in October and offer a sweet-and-salty alternative for those who aren’t quite sold on the noodles.

It has been revealed that as always, product availability can vary by warehouse, so it’s worth checking your warehouse’s stock online before making a special trip. You can also buy the Jif instant ramen at Walmart or Amazon.

But the real question is, would you give peanut butter ramen a try, or is this one food crossover you’ll happily sit out?

Snoopy, Charlie Brown and Woodstock are taking over Burger King with a latest holiday-themed menu and adorable collectibles.

It has been revealed that whenever Burger King drops a new limited-edition themed menu, I basically grab my keys and head out the door. Yes, it is that serious! I was lucky to grab a King Jr. Meal with a Hello Kitty toy the day before my local BK sold out of them completely. If you like collectibles, I’m sure you feel the same way.

Between last year’s Spongebob Meal and this year’s Mandolorian Meal, I have been really happy with all the new food drops from Burger King. I dream of eating a Whopper off of a square yellow bun again. So when I saw that Burger King will have a limited-edition Peanuts Holiday Meal this year, I cleared my schedule for the day the meal drops. Here’s everything you need to know about the festive new menu. Good grief!

Recent findings suggest that the star of the collaboration is the Peanuts Pack, a holiday feast served in a collectible Snoopy Doghouse Box. But the packaging isn’t the only fun surprise: Each Peanuts Pack also comes with one of two exclusive Snoopy holiday beanies. Talk about a cute way to top off your meal!

It has been revealed that for the main course, guests can choose between a flame-grilled Whopper with cheese or a 10-piece order of chicken nuggets. The nuggets come with a upcoming Woodstock Golden Ranch dipping sauce, which I can’t wait to try.

Here are the other upcoming treats that come in the meal:.

The Peanuts King Jr. Meal comes in its own Snoopy Doghouse Box and includes a choice of hamburger, cheeseburger or four-piece chicken nuggets. Kids can pick applesauce or french fries for a side, along with milk or apple juice. The best part? Each meal comes with one of eight collectible holiday Peanuts toys: Charlie Brown, Lucy, Linus, Sally, three Snoopy designs or a Snoopy doghouse.

One pot, four hits of lemon: Juice (limone #1) and zest (limone #2) in the cooking water, then more juice (limone #3) and zest (limone #4) to ﬁnish. The contrast of cooked and fresh citrus yields a lemon experience as wild as it gets—at least as far as pasta goes. Crème fraîche and Parmigiano-Reggiano mellow the acid into submission, delivering a creamy yet punchy ﬁnal product just begging for forks… and maybe one more squeeze of lemon.

Want some protein here? Add one pound of peeled and deveined medium shrimp to the pot as soon as the pasta turns uncomfortably al dente.

More puckery, lemony dishes this way.

Sources indicate that remove the zest from 2 lemons with a vegetable peeler in long, lengthwise strips. Chop the strips very fine. (You should have a heaping 2 Tbsp.) Transfer half the chopped zest to a large pot or Dutch oven. Reserve the remaining half.

It has been revealed that squeeze enough juice from the lemons to measure ½ cup (120 ml); reserve the remaining lemon for squeezing at the finish. Transfer ¼ cup (60 ml) of the juice to the pot with the zest and reserve the remaining juice for serving. Add 3½ cups (840 ml) water, 1 large shallot, peeled and thinly sliced, 2 Tbsp. (30 g) unsalted butter, 4 thyme sprigs, leaves stripped and stems discarded, and 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt.

Place the pot over high heat and bring to a boil. Add 1 lb. (454 g) egg noodles. (Don’t worry if they’re not fully submerged.) Cook, stirring, until the pasta is uncomfortably al dente, 5–7 minutes. Reduce the heat to medium to maintain a lively but gentle simmer and add 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and ¼ cup (60 ml) water, stirring to incorporate and create a pan sauce. Continue cooking and adding water, ¼ cup (60 ml) at a time, until there is a generous amount of sauce pooling in the pot and the noodles are al dente, 3–5 minutes more. Add ⅓ cup (80 g) crème fraîche, the remaining finely chopped lemon zest, and the reserved ¼ cup (60 ml) lemon juice. Season with kosher salt and taste. If the only flavor you’re getting is lemon, continue salting to bring out the creaminess.

According to recent reports, serve topped with a major dollop of crème fraîche and a squeeze of lemon juice. Shower with the remaining 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and pinches of flaky sea salt. (Yes, this is a lot of Parm! But stay with me here… it’s a vital balance to the punches of lemon.) Top with more thyme leaves, and if desired, cracked black pepper and chopped roasted hazelnuts.

How to make friends at freshman orientation

💡 Key Takeaways

  • What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for new member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.

Trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s fresh member orientation. Giddy, even.

The incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

Industry observers note that “I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” noted Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

Forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

“I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he said of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”.

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

According to recent reports, “It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” said Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

Cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

According to recent reports, “The congressman said that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s vital that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

According to recent reports, “This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke noted. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”.

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

“I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” said Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

Industry observers note that but just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” said Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

“I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he noted.

Sources indicate that after arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander noted he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he noted.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”.

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he remarked.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their latest workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” said Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

“They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander said.

Latest Update: Kimchi Bolognese

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve always loved Italian American food.
  • Start the Bolognese sauce: Heat 2 Tbsp.
  • ground beef, season with generous pinches of salt (at least ½ tsp.), and cook, breaking up the beef into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve always loved Italian American food. Maybe because Italian and Korean cooking have traits in common: Both are homey and resourceful, and grandmothers are revered for their signature dishes made without formal recipes. This recipe was one of the first Korean Italian fusion recipes I developed, and it makes use of my two favorite secret weapons: kimchi and fish sauce. The result is the Bolognese you know and love, but with a deep, tangy twist. Fish sauce in Italian cooking is not a fresh idea, actually—Romans have been using salted anchovies and garum, an ancient kind of fish sauce, for centuries. For an extra-special finish, I love garnishing this with baek (white) kimchi for acidity. But it’s optional, and regular kimchi (or no kimchi) works just fine, too.

More winning pasta recipes this way.

Start the Bolognese sauce: Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or pot over medium-high heat. Stir in 1 medium-yellow onion, finely diced (about 1½ cups), 2 carrots, peeled and finely diced, and 3 stalks celery, finely diced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions have softened and the edges start to brown, about 4 minutes. Stir in 4 cloves garlic, minced, and a pinch of kosher salt and cook for 30 seconds, then stir in 1 cup chopped kimchi and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook until the kimchi pieces start to soften, about 3 minutes. Pour in ½ cup red wine, increase the heat, and simmer, stirring with a wooden spoon to dislodge any bits that have stuck to the bottom, until the wine has nearly disappeared, about 2 minutes.

Add the meat: Stir in 1 lb. ground beef, season with generous pinches of salt (at least ½ tsp.), and cook, breaking up the beef into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes.

Add the tomatoes: Pour one 28-oz. can whole San Marzano tomatoes in a bowl. Using clean hands, squish the tomatoes into small pieces. Pour the tomatoes into the pot and add 1 cup beef broth or water, ½ tsp. dried Italian seasoning or dried oregano, a pinch of salt, and a few grinds of freshly ground black pepper. Bring to a simmer and lower the heat to medium-low. Gently cook, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is just thick enough to stand up on a spoon, about 20 minutes. Stir in 2 Tbsp. fish sauce and taste, then add more salt or fish sauce if needed.

In a recent development, cook the noodles and serve: In a pot of boiling salted water, cook 1 lb. spaghetti according to package instructions, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until al dente. Drain the noodles in a colander, then give the colander a shake to get rid of extra water. Divide the noodles among serving plates and spoon the Bolognese on top. Garnish with 1 cup chopped kimchi (white or regular; if using) and 2 Tbsp. chopped flat-leaf parsley and serve.

Do Ahead: Leftover Bolognese sauce (without the noodles) keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days, or in the freezer for up to 2 months.

McDonald’s is reportedly testing five hand-breaded chicken menu items in select U.S. markets, including Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and the Tucson, Arizona, area. Having taste-tested plenty of fast-food chicken sandwiches and tenders, I’ve found that the breading can make or break the entire experience. Rolling out hand-breaded chicken across thousands of restaurants, however, is easier said than done.

Recent findings suggest that the reported tests are designed to evaluate customer demand, preparation costs, and how the additional steps could affect kitchen operations. Some franchisees have reportedly expressed concerns about increased labor requirements and potential kitchen renovations.

During its November earnings call, the company confirmed that it had begun setting up operational pilots for hand-breaded chicken in the U.S. and Ireland. It also confirmed looks for larger U.S. sales tests at roughly 100 restaurants in early 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

In a recent development, A grease fire is one kitchen emergency in which instinct can work against you. Here's how to handle one safely.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most valuable things I learned in culinary school was how to work with fire without losing control of it. So much of cooking depends on knowing how far we can push the heat—getting a pan hot enough to sear steak or bringing oil just to the right temperature for a batch of fried chicken. I’ve yet to lose the little thrill of flambéing a steak au poivre or a rum-laced bananas Foster, but after years in kitchens, I have a healthy respect for high heat.

That respect is particularly warranted around the holidays, when every burner on the stove seems to be occupied, and our attention is divided between the cooking and the guests milling about in the kitchen. According to the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), Thanksgiving, Christmas Day and Christmas Eve are the three peak days of the year for home cooking fires.

According to recent reports, what makes a grease fire especially dangerous is that many of the things we’d instinctively do to put out a fire can actually cause it to spread. Fortunately, handling a grease fire safely is a fairly simple matter of knowing what to reach for and what to leave alone.

Industry observers note that whether you’re sauteing vegetables in a little olive oil or frying chicken in a Dutch oven, it’s important to recognize when your cooking fat is getting too hot. Different oils have different smoke points (the temperatures at which they begin to smoke) but if an oil continues to heat well beyond that point, it can eventually ignite without ever coming into direct contact with a flame. Overheating isn’t the only culprit, though. Oil that splashes onto a hot burner or an open flame can also catch fire, as can grease that has accumulated around the burners.

In a recent development, I find a thermometer invaluable when I’m deep-frying, but it’s crucial to keep an eye on the pan even when sauteing. It’s frighteningly easy to get distracted chopping the next ingredient or chatting with your dinner guests. If you notice smoke rising from your pan, turn off the burner immediately.

In a recent development, should the oil catch fire, leave the pan where it is. As instinctive as it may be to move it to the sink, carrying burning oil through the kitchen is a serious burn hazard, and risks spreading the fire.

Sources indicate that the most vital thing to remember about a grease fire is that water will only make it worse. Most of us are familiar with the rather unpleasant sensation of hot oil spattering onto our hands when moisture finds its way into a sizzling pan. The science behind that reaction is the same here: Water sinks and turns rapidly to steam, agitating the oil. When the oil is burning, that sudden expansion can send flames and droplets of burning oil well beyond the stovetop.

A fire extinguisher may seem like the obvious thing to reach for, but not all extinguishers are suited for grease fires. Class K extinguishers are designed specifically for fires involving cooking oils and fats, and they can be useful if you have one and know how to use it safely. For a small grease fire contained within a pan, though, there’s a simpler (and considerably less expensive) piece of kitchen equipment that can do the job: a metal lid.

In a recent development, both the NFPA and the U.S. Fire Administration recommend keeping one nearby when cooking. A small, contained grease fire can often be extinguished simply by depriving it of oxygen. Provided the flames haven’t spread beyond the pan, and you can approach it safely, here’s what to do:.

According to recent reports, if covering the pan doesn’t extinguish the flames, it’s notable to recognize that the situation is beyond your control. Get everyone outside and call 911.

I Tried Dolly Parton’s Appalachian Apple Stack Cake, and It’s One-of-a-Kind

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This warmly spiced cake from Dolly Parton can be made days in advance and is the perfect addition to your holiday dessert table.
  • According to recent reports, all the adjectives I imagine to describe Dolly Parton, I can also attribute to this one-of-a-kind cake from her cookbook.
  • An apple stack cake is a popular Appalachian dessert comprised of layers of spiced cake and apple filling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

This warmly spiced cake from Dolly Parton can be made days in advance and is the perfect addition to your holiday dessert table.

According to recent reports, all the adjectives I imagine to describe Dolly Parton, I can also attribute to this one-of-a-kind cake from her cookbook. It’s unlike anything I have ever made before, but at the same time it is warm and comforting, all while standing tall in a class by itself. With scents of apple, vanilla, cinnamon and allspice, it’s certainly a recipe to try this time of year and could even be a great addition to a Dolly-inspired meal.

An apple stack cake is a popular Appalachian dessert comprised of layers of spiced cake and apple filling. Dolly’s version uses molasses in the “crust,” aka cake layers and fresh apples in the filling (whereas other recipes often call for dried apples).

The original recipe for Dolly’s apple stack “cake” was actually referred to as a “pie” in her 1986 cookbook Dollywood Presents Tennessee Mountain Home Cooking. I wasn’t exactly sure why there was a crisscrossing of names until I started to prepare this unique recipe. The flour and butter in the “crust” layers are cut together using a pastry blender, much like you might do when making a traditional pie crust. Then, eggs, molasses, sugar, milk and spices are also added. This transforms the recipe into a thicker batter, similar to a scone or even a quick bread. The filling is like a thick, spiced applesauce with a thin layer spread between each stack.

I found the directions in the original recipe to be a bit confusing. For example, there was no mention of using cold butter even though the dough starts off more like pastry crust. In the instructions below, I added a bit more detail in order to clarify the process for anyone who wants to try making this special Dolly dessert.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, in a large bowl, sift together flour and baking soda. Cut the cold butter into cubes and then use a pastry blender to cut the cubes into the flour mixture until it looks like coarse sand. In a separate bowl, beat together eggs, molasses, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon and milk.

Sources indicate that add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture and mix until it looks like a thick dough. Cover the bottom of 6 round cake pans with parchment. Grease and flour the cake pans. Evenly divide the dough among the cake pans and, with floured hands, press it out toward the edges of each pan.

Sources indicate that bake at 300°F for 10 to 15 minutes, or until golden brown. Cool in the pans for 10 minutes, then remove to a wire rack and continue cooling.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Cook the apples slowly in water until soft. Strain any remaining liquid. This should yield about 1 cup of pulp. Add sugar, cinnamon and allspice. Cook over low heat until the sugar dissolves and the mixture thickens.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Place the filling between layers, and stack one layer on top of the other. This recipe will make two 3-layer cakes or one 6-layer cake. This cake is best after it sits for two or three days. Dust with powdered sugar before serving, if desired. Yield: 10 to 12 servings.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that I was glad I did a little research before making this recipe to learn that it’s best to add parchment to the bottom of each cake pan to avoid sticking. Because I did this, the layers released easily from the pans, so I highly recommend this step. I also took a tip from the Taste of Home Apple Stack Cake recipe to add powdered sugar on top before serving. Since this cake needed a little something to finish off the look, this was just the right move. Plus, I doubt Dolly would disagree with a little extra accessorizing!

According to recent reports, I agree that this recipe tastes best after it sits for a couple of days. The flavor of the molasses in the batter melds with the warm spices to create a dessert that is truly in a class by itself. Given that it can be made in advance, that is a great way to get a head start on a holiday meal and enjoy a stress-free treat that is already done and ready to enjoy. Serve with a scoop of ice cream or a dollop of whipped cream!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.
  • Sources indicate that house Republicans had hoped that upcoming congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

Sources indicate that house Republicans had hoped that upcoming congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” remarked Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the new lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

Latest maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, mentioned he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

It has been revealed that advocates for a fresh map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley remarked he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

In a recent development, democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Upcoming York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Sources indicate that officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

In a recent development, it’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass latest maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where new maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, stated last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

It has been revealed that in Latest Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Recent findings suggest that democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their new majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he remarked Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to fresh maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he mentioned.

When I came across Made In Cookware’s set, I knew it was a sign that I, too, could adopt this sophisticated French look. These knives are manufactured in Thiers, France, a region known for knife-making, which speaks to their aesthetic and craftsmanship. I love that they’re non-serrated; the sharp edges maintain the integrity of meat and can be sharpened once dull. These steak knives are also full tang, which means they’re constructed with a single rod of stainless steel from tip to handle. And speaking of the handle—the feature that attracted me to this set in the first place—they come in several materials, including olive wood, black polymer, and (my pick) pearlescent acetate. — Melissa Knific, contributing editor.

Recent findings suggest that what is a martini glass if not a tiny birdbath for my olives? These Year and Day glasses are my favorite kind: classic and elevated, but durable. They’re great for anything you’d serve up, and the best part is that I can set them in the dishwasher at the end of the night. —Casey Hendricks, executive director of audience development.

Recent findings suggest that A woman in her late 20s who starts her mornings with a mug of bone broth as the weather gets cold—I know I’m a cliché. But this chicken bone broth from Fond, specifically the turmeric and black pepper variety, truly does start my day off on the right note. There’s eight grams of protein per cup, sure, but my favorite part is that it’s made without alliums (like garlic and onion) so it’s especially kind to my tummy. Instead, the broth gets its flavor from carrots, turmeric root, celery, lemon juice, cracked black pepper, and thyme. All the vegetables Fond uses are organic and they use 100% pasture-raised chicken, so it’s as close to making my own bone broth at home as I can get, without having to simmer a pot for 18 hours. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

M6HG Instant Hot Countertop Reverse Osmosis Water Filter.

Sources indicate that there were a couple of things happening at my house at the same time: First, my wife’s lovely and enormous collection of houseplants continued growing; second, we decided to get a water softener to fight against the notoriously hard water in my part of Newly introduced Jersey. Those two things don’t go together well because softened water and its added sodium can be bad for plants long term. A reverse osmosis system is one way to fight against that, but we didn’t have the budget (or really the need) for a whole-home RO system, nor did we have the space under our sink for one of those. Enter Waterdrop’s countertop RO. The M6HG has an autofilling pitcher that makes plant care convenient, but it’s also turned out it’s getting more use than our fridge filter for drinking. Water comes out a chilly 48 degrees and measures precisely to 4, 8, or 16 ounces (which my kids love for some reason). It also dispenses at 77℉, 113℉ (supposedly good for baby formula), 131℉, 149℉, 167℉, 185℉ (for delicate tea), and 203℉ (for French press or pour-over coffee). Oh yeah, it’s on massive sale for Black Friday. — Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor.

I never grew up with advent calendars, but I can totally see what the fuss is about. My family and I take such joy opening up a window of surprise every morning. Since the advent calendars in our home are usually food-related, we’ll enjoy the treat together later in the evening, with varying degrees of jostling, depending on what it is. Well, looks like the 2026 holiday season will be another one of us throwing elbows because we have our hands on BonBon’s magnificent Lighthouse Advent Calendar. No paper windows here! The cool Swedish confectionary’s calendar is actually a long tower filled with 24 individually wrapped, numbered mini bags of vegan gummies. The daily candy should be a mix of BonBon’s exclusive fresh flavors as well as its beloved classics. I think my Swedish husband and daughter are already losing their minds (it’s only November) and I’m already fearing for our next dental visit, but it is giving this exceptionally fast holiday season a good reason to stop and appreciate a fun, sweet moment every day. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food director.

Industry observers note that ’Tis the season for...soup. My Dutch oven and I have been on a tear making favorites like white chicken chili, chicken-lentil soup, and tons of minestrone. In my attempt to “be frugal,” I’ve been bringing my soups to work for lunch in my, yes, ludicrously capacious bag, and more specifically, my 20 oz. insulated thermos by Hydroflask. It’s truly the perfect size for a lunch-appropriate portion and keeps my soup warm from morning until around 1 p.m. when it’s time to eat between meetings. It’s completely leak-proof which is crucial for a soup commute. And, it’s dishwasher safe, so when I come home after work, I can just throw it in the dishwasher to use all over again the next day. A small investment for a considerably more delightful desk lunch. —June Kim, executive editor.

Limited Edition Peppermint Mocha Barista.

I’m not really a pumpkin spice latte girl, but a peppermint mocha is a seasonal drink I can definitely get behind—so when I heard that Táche, the brand behind my favorite pistachio milk, had come out with a Peppermint Mocha flavor, I was very eager to try it. Sure enough, it was love at first sip. It tastes deeply chocolatey thanks to the addition of Dutch-processed cocoa, and has just enough peppermint flavor to feel festive and balanced without veering into toothpaste territory. Industry observers note that I’m often hesitant to use pre-made, packaged products when it comes to cooking. One could say I’m a bit of a control freak, but I’m not opposed to a shortcut, especially when it’s after 7 p.m. on a weeknight and I still need to get dinner on the table.

I’m looking forward to dipping into the lavender-scented “Calm” blend ahead of the forthcoming hectic holiday season! —Rebecca Firkser, test kitchen editor.

  • It has been revealed that after playing Tetris in my oven an hour before a holiday party, I’m always relieved I decided to serve a cheese board as the appetizer.
  • So, I sat down with the experts: Molly Browne, dean of mongers at Cheese State University and education director at Dairy Farmers of Wisconsin, and Emilia D’Albero, the first American ever crowned World’s Best Cheesemonger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

I chatted with two cheesemongers to find out exactly what I should be putting on my cheese spreads this holiday season. Surprisingly, a classic cheddar isn't at the top!

It has been revealed that after playing Tetris in my oven an hour before a holiday party, I’m always relieved I decided to serve a cheese board as the appetizer. Cheese boards don’t require much time to put together (and take up zero oven space), but I seem to linger on the cheese selection, always asking myself the same question: Which cheeses would everyone like to eat?

So, I sat down with the experts: Molly Browne, dean of mongers at Cheese State University and education director at Dairy Farmers of Wisconsin, and Emilia D’Albero, the first American ever crowned World’s Best Cheesemonger. They gave me the scoop on putting together the perfect holiday cheese board. Molly and Emilia recommend three to five cheeses per board, representing a variety of milk types, styles and flavors.

According to recent reports, but which cheese should I buy that everyone would like? More specifically, what feels indulgent but won’t alienate picky eaters? I expected Molly and Emilia to recommend some extremely specific, hard-to-find cheeses, but both suggested varieties I could pick up at the grocery store.

According to Molly, the best cheese for a holiday cheese board that appeals to all ages is butterkase. This semi-firm cow’s milk cheese is creamy, smooth, relatively mild and exceptionally buttery—hence its German name, which translates to “butter cheese.” (If you’re as chronically online as I am, you may have heard of butterkase from @courtneycookinsta, who famously stuffs butterkase in a warm sweet potato and eats it for lunch.).

In a recent development, butterkase is typically aged for only about a month, so it doesn’t have much funk, making it approachable for the under-10 and over-60 crowd. “I’ve seen my own child pick up a piece of it and eat it like an apple on multiple occasions,” says Molly. But because of butterkase’s slight complexity, Molly explained that it won’t leave those in the middle feeling devoid of flavor or a good eating experience, so it’s a safe bet for a charcuterie board.

Butterkase is made in Wisconsin and sold nationwide, but if you’re having trouble finding it, Gouda is a good alternative, especially Emilia’s recommendation: aged Gouda.

It has been revealed that aged Gouda is a Dutch-style hard cheese that matures anywhere from nine months to five years. As Gouda matures, the soft paste turns firm and speckles with those irresistible crunchy crystals. It takes on an indulgent butterscotch flavor, with subtle tropical notes, so it’s on the sweeter side. The longer the Gouda ages, the more intense those characteristics become. “In my experience, nobody’s ever turned down an aged Gouda,” says Emilia.

According to recent reports, because it’s especially buttery and mild, butterkase pairs well with tangy, acidic foods, like olives, the foods on a relish tray and all kinds of pickles: classic pickles, pickled vegetables and pickled fruit. Their acidity cuts through the richness of the cheese. Butterkase would also be a fantastic addition to a supper club board. Its soft texture is great on crisp crackers studded with nuts and fruits, with a German mustard nearby.

For wine and cheese pairings, opt for something light and refreshing, like Prosecco or an unoaked chardonnay, to balance the richness of the cheese. Even a bottle of inexpensive champagne makes the cheese board feel a little fancier.

Slice butterkase while it’s still cold from the fridge. If it sits for a while, butterkase can become soft enough to spread, making it difficult to slice. As a general rule, Molly and Emilia recommend slicing harder cheeses in advance to get ahead of cheese board prep. Keep backup portions in the fridge to promptly replenish the board as the night goes on.

Recent findings suggest that aged Gouda pairs well with sweeter fruit jams, chocolate, candied pecans and even tropical fruits like mango. Fruit-and-nut studded crackers work just as well with aged Gouda as they do with butterkase. For dessert, try pairing the cheese with brownies or caramelly stroopwafels. Drink pairings range from red wine to spiced rum.

While there are guidelines for pairing, Emilia encourages people to step out of their comfort zone and explore out-of-the-box options. “There’s no wrong answer to pairing,” she claims. “People tend to think that they have to only pair fancy things with cheese, and honestly, some of the best pairings I’ve had have just been snacks or things I love that are lying around the house.” Take a cue from Emilia’s cheese competition days: Try the cheese with whatever you have in the kitchen; you may discover an unexpected favorite. “Get weird with it,” says Emilia.

They wandered from market to market, weaving through the stalls and sharing everything that caught their eye. Their hands-down favorite was the khanom tom, which her grandmother grew up buying from a street vendor in Bangkok as an after-school treat. Traditionally made with both fresh coconut and coconut milk, the bite-size sweets are chewy, fragrant, and irresistible.

Industry observers note that thankfully, khanom tom are easy to pull together at home and require no special equipment or technique. Glutinous rice flour gives the dough a pleasantly bouncy texture, and a palm sugar and coconut filling imparts a rich, caramel-like sweetness. After a quick boil, each ball is rolled in shredded fresh coconut for a soft, snowy finish.

Breaking: Is It Safe to Eat from a Charcuterie Board That’s Been Out All Afternoon?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Charcuterie boards are a party favorite, but how long can they safely sit out?
  • Industry observers note that I totally understand the excitement that comes from spying a gorgeous charcuterie board at a gathering.
  • In a recent development, food safety was a big deal in my studies, and all those lessons about safe cooking temperatures, proper food handling and food storage have stuck with me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Charcuterie boards are a party favorite, but how long can they safely sit out? Here's what to know before you grab another bite of that wilted cheese.

Industry observers note that I totally understand the excitement that comes from spying a gorgeous charcuterie board at a gathering. Between the cheeses, the cured meats and all the little finger foods, there are too many potential combinations to wonder how long everything has been sitting out. But as a registered dietitian, I can’t help thinking about it!

In a recent development, food safety was a big deal in my studies, and all those lessons about safe cooking temperatures, proper food handling and food storage have stuck with me. After all, cut a few corners here or let food sit out a little too long there, and you could find yourself in a real pickle—one where you risking spoiling all that delicious food you took time to prepare.

Recent findings suggest that so, how long can a charcuterie board safely sit out before it’s time to show it the bin? With the holidays in full swing and cheese boards popping up at just about every gathering, these food safety tips will keep you snacking happily and safely all season long.

Industry observers note that yes, but you’ll want to keep an eye on the clock! Most perishable items on a charcuterie board—including soft cheeses, deli meats, chilled dips and cut fruit—shouldn’t sit at room temperature for more than two hours. If the temperature is above 90°F (like at an outdoor summer party), that window shrinks to just one hour.

It has been revealed that harmful bacteria can multiply rapidly when perishable foods spend too much time in the temperature danger zone, which is between 40°F and 140°F. And unfortunately food doesn’t have to look or smell spoiled to be unsafe to eat.

According to recent reports, some charcuterie boards are designed to keep food chilled, with built-in compartments for ice packs or trays that sit over ice. If the perishable foods are kept at 40°F or below, they can stay out a little longer without entering the temperature danger zone.

One thing to keep in mind: The clock starts when the perishable foods come out of the refrigerator, not when guests start digging in. If a charcuterie board has been sitting out for more than two hours, it’s safest to toss the perishable items rather than save them for later.

According to recent reports, and if you’re a guest and aren’t sure how long the board has been sitting out, you have a couple options. You can either casually ask the host, or you can skip the perishable items altogether and stick with shelf-stable munchies like crackers, seasoned nuts and pretzels.

Recent findings suggest that sort of! Hard cheeses like Parmesan, Manchego and aged Gouda handle room temperature better than soft cheeses like Brie, fresh goat cheese, fresh mozzarella and cream cheese.

That’s because hard cheeses contain less moisture, so they’re a little less hospitable to the harmful bacteria that can make you sick. Soft cheeses have more moisture, so they’re more perishable and should follow the same strict two-hour rule as other refrigerated foods.

Sources indicate that while hard cheeses are a safer bet than soft varieties, that doesn’t mean they can sit out indefinitely! They’re still subject to food safety concerns, so if you’re not sure how long the board has been sitting out, it’s safest to skip the perishable items regardless of the cheese type.

You can’t always tell if food is safe to eat just by looking at it, but there are a few visible signs that a charcuterie board may have been sitting out for a while. You might notice cheeses sweating or getting extra soft or oily, or you might see sliced meats starting to look dried out around the edges. Cut fruit may also turn mushy or discolored as it sits.

Recent findings suggest that not everything on a cheese board carries the same food safety risk. When in doubt, don’t take a chance on foods that need refrigeration. You can always fill your plate with the shelf-stable nuts, crackers and whole fruit instead.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re hosting, put out smaller portions of cheeses and meats and replenish the board as needed. That way, you can keep the extra food refrigerated until it’s time to serve more, rather than letting everything sit out for hours.

Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
