Industry News: Latest Discovery Could Transform How We Treat Chronic Back Pain

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Restoring a protein that declines in aging spinal discs reduced DNA damage in human cells in the lab, revealing a potential latest target for back pain treatments.
  • For people living with persistent back pain, everyday activities such as walking, bending, or even sitting comfortably can become difficult.
  • Spinal discs are cushion-like structures between vertebrae that allow the spine to move.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Restoring a protein that declines in aging spinal discs reduced DNA damage in human cells in the lab, revealing a potential latest target for back pain treatments.

For people living with persistent back pain, everyday activities such as walking, bending, or even sitting comfortably can become difficult. New research from the University of Utah points toward a possible way to address one of the underlying causes of age-related back pain by protecting the cells that keep spinal discs healthy.

Spinal discs are cushion-like structures between vertebrae that allow the spine to move. In a study published in Aging Cell, researchers found that older and damaged discs contained lower levels of a protein called BLST, which is encoded by the ZNF865 gene. The study is the first to characterize the function of both the gene and its protein.

To understand whether declining BLST levels contribute to disc deterioration, the researchers used CRISPR, a gene-editing tool that can be used to regulate the activity of specific genes. Restoring BLST production in human disc cells reduced signs of cellular aging and DNA damage, while decreasing its activity in mouse and rat models led to disc degeneration and pain-related behaviors. The findings suggest that BLST helps maintain healthy spinal discs by protecting cells from damage and dysfunction as they age.

“This paper directly reveals a novel understanding that DNA damage is a driver of back pain, and that we can regulate BLST therapeutically with CRISPR,” said Robby D. Bowles, the study’s lead researcher and an associate professor of biomedical engineering. “Back pain is the number three leading cause of disability as measured by disability-adjusted life years, only behind cardiac disease and drug use disorders.”.

Although increasing BLST activity could eventually offer a way to prevent or treat age-related back pain, additional preclinical studies and, ultimately, clinical trials are needed to determine whether targeting the protein with CRISPR is safe and effective in people.

The research brought together Bowles and members of his laboratory in the John and Marcia Price College of Engineering, specialists in orthopedics and arthritis at the Spencer Fox Eccles School of Medicine, and researchers at Huntsman Cancer Institute at the University of Utah.

Because DNA damage is involved in numerous diseases, the discovery could have applications well beyond spinal health.

“It has been the highlight of my career to work on a protein that was unknown and be the first to identify its function,” Bowles remarked. “While this work focuses on its application to back pain, the mechanisms identified have the potential to be applied to treat cancer, neurodegeneration, and any disease in which DNA damage is involved.”.

Further research is needed to establish whether the protective mechanisms observed in spinal disc cells also play a role in age-related cancers.

“The fact that a single gene can restore normal cell function and reverse aging-related effects is incredible,” said Jason Gertz, a professor in the Department of Oncological Sciences at the University of Utah and co-leader of the Genomics, Epigenetics, and Metabolism Program at Huntsman Cancer Institute. “BLST is widely expressed across tissues and could be a promising target for cancer treatment and prevention, since boosting BLST activity should improve the repair of DNA damage and the overall health of aging cells.”.

Reference: “ZNF865 (BLST) a Novel Regulator of DNA Damage and Cell Senescence in Back Pain” by Christian Lewis, Hunter Levis, Jonah Holbrook, Jacob T. Polaski, Timothy D. Jacobsen, Josh Mizels, Molly Czachor, Sarah E. Gullbrand, Brian Diekman, James C. Iatridis, Jason Gertz, Brandon Lawrence and Robby D. Bowles, 9 October 2026, Aging Cell. DOI: 10.1111/acel.70754.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.
  • Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

It has been revealed that the race was reshaped by the Golden State’s latest voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

According to recent reports, the rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In a recent development, in her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she mentioned in a statement.

According to recent reports, the race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Industry observers note that calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

It has been revealed that one incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Sources indicate that two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

Study Finds Artemis Astronauts Will Enjoy Moon-Grown Potatoes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By now, references to Mark Watney and how he grew potatoes in Martian soil have become a tired clichÃ©.
  • This is good news for space agencies like NASA that are actively planning to send astronauts back to the Moon, and this time, to stay.
  • To support long-term missions far from Earth, where opportunities for resupply will be fewer and farther between, a degree of self-sufficiency is required.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By now, references to Mark Watney and how he grew potatoes in Martian soil have become a tired clichÃ©. Nevertheless, one can't help but recall the scene whenever news breaks about the latest experiment that examines the potential of growing plants in extraterrestrial soils. The latest comes from Oregon State University (OSU), where researchers have shown that potatoes grown in lunar soil simulant (amended with organic matter) are safe to eat and grow just as well as those produced on Earth.

This is good news for space agencies like NASA that are actively planning to send astronauts back to the Moon, and this time, to stay. Through the Artemis Program, crews will land around the South Pole-Aitken Basin and begin constructing a permanent base that will enable regular missions in the future (about one per year). China's National Space Agency (CNSA) and Roscosmos also strategy on building a base - the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) - in the same region by the end of the decade.

To support long-term missions far from Earth, where opportunities for resupply will be fewer and farther between, a degree of self-sufficiency is required. Whereas the International Space Station (ISS) is resupplied regularly and emergency supplies can be dispatched within hours, missions to the Moon will take at least three days to arrive. As such, any sustained program of exploration on the Moon must rely on In-Situ Resource Utilization(ISRU) as much as possible - i.e., using local resources for building materials and providing astronauts with water and food.

In a recent development, research in the past few decades has led to methods for 3D printing habitats and other facilities using lunar regolith. This can be combined with a bonding agent to create "lunacrete," or sintered with microwaves to create molten ceramic. Either material is then deposited layer by layer by construction robots to form walls and other structural elements. While hydroponics remain a viable way to grow plants (as astronauts do aboard the ISS), the real question is whether Earth plants can be grown in lunar regolith and other extraterrestrial soils.

In a recent development, led by Aymeric Goyer, a professor with OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, the Oregon team used lunar regolith simulants with different levels of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich organic soil produced when earthworms break down organic matter. With support from NASA's Johnson Space Center Simulant Development Lab, the team produced healthy potatoes with yields comparable to crops grown by farmers in Oregon (the 4th largest potato producer in the U.S.).

Sources indicate that goyer and his teams specifically selected potatoes because they produce more calories per square meter of soil than many other crops. They also offer substantial nutritional value: one medium skin-on potato (148 g/5.3 oz) provides roughly 110 calories, 26 g of carbohydrates, 3 g of protein, and 2 g of fiber. They are also naturally fat-free, gluten-free, cholesterol-free, and are therefore considered a practical staple food for long-duration space missions.

Since lunar regolith varies across the Moon, the researchers tested five simulants representing lunar mare (fine-grained basaltic soil) and lunar highland (feldspar-rich volcanic soil) regions. They also included soil from Hermiston, Oregon, which produces the world's highest potato yield. The results showed that potato plants grown in simulants containing 30% vermicompost grew as well as those cultivated in Earth soils. In other samples, plants grown without vermicompost were severely stunted and had underdeveloped root systems.

It has been revealed that the "Moon Village" concept, conceived by MIT in collaboration with the ESA and Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. Credit: ESA/Skidmore, Owings & Merrill.

Lastly, those grown with 5% to 15% vermicompost highlighted only partial growth. As Goyer said in an OSU press release:.

We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter. That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.

According to recent reports, the results also showed that the potatoes grown in lunar regolith simulants maintained their nutritional quality, with no statistically significant increase in naturally occurring potato toxins (glycoalkaloids) often associated with green discoloration. Lunar regolith still presents many challenges for plant growth, which include extremely fine-grained dust and elevated levels of heavy metals.

In a recent development, but the researchers are confident that adding organic matter helps bind heavy metals, preventing them from damaging roots, interfering with growth, or leaching into the potatoes themselves. In the future, astronauts could bring compost to the Moon, along with Earth worms, to create their own fertilizer, augmenting soil collected during surface trips to grow their food.

According to recent reports, "We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," said David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab. Their results are reported in a paper, "Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants," that appeared in npj Microgravity. Another paper, which reports the results of experiments involving 10 potato varieties to identify which grow best in lunar soil, will be released.

Eater Awards celebrated the best restaurants, chefs, and more of 2026.

It has been revealed that if you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

What a night. On Sunday, November 15, the winners of the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, celebrated together at Nine Orchard in NYC. More than 200 chefs, restaurateurs, bartenders, and friends of Eater — many of whom traveled across the country to be there — partook in live portraiture, custom engraving, and, of course, plenty of food and drink.

Industry observers note that now in its 17th year, the Eater Awards recognize the year’s best upcoming restaurants, bakeries, bars, dishes, and chefs in markets across the U.S.. More than 30 Eater staffers and contributors spent months traveling to 44 cities to weigh contenders on food, service, atmosphere, and the stories behind them. The prize? A tomato can trophy. And yes, they’re real.

It has been revealed that the night started off strong with photos at the tomato can-wrapped step-and-repeat and a welcome shot of Zbiotics, before guests headed up to the roof of Nine Orchard for panoramic views and more fun. The party was filled with unique moments, from custom lighter engraving presented by Toast to live water color portraits presented by Capital One. Rounds of dishes inspired by the winning restaurants were passed.

In a recent development, A champagne toast commemorated the resiliency of the hospitality industry. “Thank you for what you do, every single day, to bolster your team, your community, and the restaurant industry at large,” said Eater editor in chief Stephanie Wu.

Rose Previte of DC’s Maydan, Medina, and Souk, and 2026 Best Latest Restaurant winner Maydan Market LA joined Wu on stage to present the first-ever Pre Shift Future of Hospitality Award to Maison Bar à Vins. This peer-voted award honors one winner whose work is particularly forward-thinking, challenges conventions, sets new standards, and points toward the future of hospitality. Matt Conroy and Jason Chavenson took home the surprise award.

“It’s really amazing to win an award like this that’s voted by everybody here and, you know, so many people we look up to, so it’s really incredible,” said Matt Conroy.

All attendees received an Eater tote filled with editor-curated products including Bubs candy, Zbiotics, TimeSavvy’s self-care and travel essentials kit, sweet matcha drops and fiery garlic chili sauce from Bokksu, a Wood Cabin candle from Keap Candles, chef socks from Cargo Crew, and a gift certificate for a pair of shoes from Snibbs.

It truly was a great night celebrating the hard work these chefs and their teams put into creating the best dining experiences of the year. Feeling FOMO? Check out the full list of winners and see for yourself what made these restaurants and chefs stand out.
